items.text: System.out.println is a library method that prints its argument followed by a line terminator ('print line').
println(String x) behaves as though it calls print(x) and then println(); println() terminates the current line by writing the line separator string.
Evaluate the argument, print its characters at the current position, then write the line separator so the cursor moves to the beginning of the next line.
Output is the value's characters followed by a line break: println("Hello, "); println("World!"); prints two lines.
One call appends the text and a line separator to the output; the cursor ends at the start of the next line; no variable changes and nothing is returned.
System.out.println(s); is a statement, so its line of output appears at its own place in the sequence.
println("s") outputs exactly the characters between the quotes and then ends the line.
print leaves the cursor on the line; println ends it; several prints followed by one println make one line.
println prints numbers with all their digits and always ends the line; printf formats each value by its conversion code and ends the line only where the format has %n or \n.
Purpose: produce one complete line of output, e.g. each result on its own line, or end a line built with print.
Replacing println with print joins the next output onto the same line (a typical logic error); the characters printed stay the same.
Use println when each output item belongs on its own line or to end a line; use print to continue a line and printf to control number formatting.

items.text: Nesting puts an if or if-else inside a branch of another if-else; an else-if chain is the common case where the else branch is itself an if.
if-else extends if with a second block that runs exactly when the condition is false.
Every if statement requires an else.
An if statement may stand alone; the else part is optional.
if (x > 0); System.out.println("positive"); prints only for positive x.
The ; ends the if with an empty statement, so the next line always runs.
An inner if runs its body whenever its own condition is true, even if the outer if condition is false.
The inner if is part of the outer branch: it is reached, and its condition tested, only when the outer condition is true.
Ends the output with print and expects it to appear right away.
Finish a line of print calls with println; some systems hold print output until a newline is printed.
Indenting several statements under an if or for makes them all part of its body, even without braces.
Without braces only the first statement belongs to the if/for; the rest run once, after it.
An output statement that names the same variable twice (WRITE y, x, y) prints it only once.
Each expression in the output list is printed, so a repeated variable prints its value each time.
println with nothing to print can be written System.out.println; without the parentheses.
A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.
"10" - 1 or "6" * "2" works because the strings look like numbers.
Arithmetic operators other than + are not defined for Strings; a String of digits must first be converted to a number, e.g. with Integer.parseInt.
Nested conditionals are if or if-else statements placed inside a branch of another conditional; an else-if chain is the common special case.

An if/if-else is a statement, so it can be the body (branch) of another conditional; without braces an else belongs to the innermost if to which it might belong, so braces should be used to resolve ambiguities.
Test the outer condition; only if control enters the branch that contains the inner if is the inner condition tested; after the inner statement, control leaves the outer statement too.
The output is the action of the single path whose conditions all hold along the way: if (a > b) { if (b > c) X; else Y; } else Z; runs X when a > b > c, Y when a > b and b <= c, and Z otherwise.
One execution evaluates the conditions along one path only (outer, then possibly inner) and applies one leaf action; conditions on other paths are never evaluated.
Nesting puts an if or if-else inside a branch of another if-else; when the inner statement fills the else branch it forms an else-if chain.
The dangling-else ambiguity arises when ifs are nested without braces: if <e1> if <e2> A else B attaches else to the inner if.
For more than two mutually exclusive alternatives a chain of if-else statements works, but a switch tests one expression against many values directly.
Plan: decision tree - refine a case analysis step by step (e.g. find the smallest of three values, classify a value into ranges).

Combining if (c1) { if (c2) S; } into if (c1 && c2) S; preserves behaviour when there are no else parts; adding or removing braces around an inner if can move an else to a different if. Swapping some branches can keep the specification only on certain inputs.

Nest conditionals when a second test only makes sense once the first has succeeded or when cases form a tree; use && for a simple conjunction, an else-if chain for mutually exclusive ranges, and a switch for many discrete values; one or two levels usually suffice.

rule broken: Without braces an else pairs with the innermost if, whatever the indentation. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: if (a) if (b) X; else Y; written with else under the outer if: Y runs when a is true and b false, not when a is false.

items.text: After the matching case runs, the switch ends even without break.
Without break, statements in switch blocks fall through into the following cases.
Selection statement: `switch (expr) { case v1: ...; break; ... default: ... }` chooses among many alternatives by the value of one expression.

The selector is an int-like (char, byte, short, int), String or enum expression. Case labels are distinct constants of that type, and default is optional. Control jumps to the matching label (or to default, or past the switch), and the case statements usually end with break. Without a break, execution falls through into the statements of the next case; default runs when no case matches.

Order: evaluate the selector once; compare it with the case constants; jump to the matching label (else default, else skip the switch). Then execute the statements from there in order, through later labels, until a break or the closing brace.
A switch statement has no value. Its result is the effect of the case(s) run: with `day = 3`, the S&W day switch prints Wed. Without breaks, day = 5 would print Fri, then Sat.
One execution evaluates the selector once (any side effect in it happens once) and runs the statements of one entry point and any cases it falls into. It changes only what those statements change.
A switch replaces an if-else chain only when every test is `expr == constant` on the same expression. Range tests such as the income-bracket chain (`income < 47450`) must stay an if-else chain.
Each case is normally ended by break, which exits the switch body. Leaving it out makes that case fall into the next. Inside a loop, that break exits the switch, not the loop.

Plan: multiway dispatch or lookup. It maps one discrete value (day number, menu choice, character) to one of several actions or results. Grouped labels (`case "apple": case "banana":`) map several values to one action.

When every case ends with break, reordering the cases does not change behaviour (labels are distinct constants). Removing one break changes behaviour for that value only. Adding a default changes only values with no matching label.

Use switch for more than two mutually exclusive alternatives decided by equality of one int, char, String or enum value. Use an if-else chain for ranges, doubles or unrelated conditions. Use an array lookup (S&W 1.4) when each case only selects a value.

rule broken: Without break, execution falls through into the following cases. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Any selector value whose case lacks a break: the following cases' statements also run (e.g. both Fri and Sat printed).

rule broken: Values that match no case do nothing unless a default is present. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: An out-of-range selector (day = 7) with no default: nothing happens, and a variable assigned only in the cases may stay unassigned.

rule broken: Case labels must be distinct compile-time constants of the selector type, and the selector may not be double, float, long or boolean. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Duplicate `case 1:` labels, a variable as a label, or `switch (x)` with x a double.
rule broken: A String selector is dereferenced. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: Switching on a String variable that is null throws NullPointerException.

items.text: Array copy: a second, independent array holding the same elements as the first.
To copy an array, create a new array of the same length and copy the elements one by one: double[] b = new double[N]; for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) b[i] = a[i]; (java.util.Arrays.copyOf does the same).
Sequencing: new creates the second array first, then the loop copies a[0], a[1], ... in order into b[0], b[1], ...; after the loop, a and b are separate arrays with equal elements.
Result: after copying, b[i] == a[i] for every i, but a == b is false; after b[0] = 9, a[0] is unchanged.
State transition: each pass of the copy loop sets one element of the new array and leaves the original unchanged.
The copy is a traversal of every index of the original.
b = a makes an alias of the same array; a copy is a different array: changes through one are not seen through the other.
Plan: copy an array when the original must stay unchanged while the copy is modified (for example shuffling or sorting a copy).
Conservation: changing the copy never changes the original, and the reverse; with an alias every change is shared.
When an algorithm must change an array but the original is still needed, work on a copy made with new and a loop (or Arrays.copyOf).
rule broken: Assignment copies the reference, not the elements. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: b = a is used as a copy and then b is modified while a is expected to stay unchanged

A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.

y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
Writes a + b = c; or 7 = a; as if = were a math equation.
The left side of an assignment must be a single variable; only the right side can be an expression.
Writes int x = 5; ... int x = 10; to change x.
A declaration gives a variable its name and type; a later change of value is an assignment statement such as x = 10;, not a second declaration.
b = a exchanges the values of a and b.
b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.
x = y checks whether x and y are equal.
x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
a = b copies the value of a into b.
Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.
Comparison (relational) operators ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= are mixed-type operators: they take two operands of a numeric type and produce a boolean.

==, !=, <, <=, >, >= are defined for each primitive numeric type and produce a boolean; they have lower precedence than arithmetic and higher than boolean operators; < and > are not defined for Strings, and == on non-primitive types compares identity.
Evaluate the left operand (including its arithmetic), then the right operand; if their types differ, promote the narrower one (int to double); then compare and produce true or false.
The result is a boolean: (2 <= 2) is true, 2 < 2 is false, (x < 3.1) is true for int x = 3; any comparison involving NaN, even NaN == NaN, is false.
A comparison changes no variable and only returns a boolean, unlike =, which changes the value of the variable on its left.
A comparison is itself an expression whose value is a boolean, so it can appear anywhere a boolean is needed, including on the right of an assignment (boolean ok = x > y;).
Comparisons are the building blocks of conditions: together with boolean logic they provide the basis for decision-making.
Comparisons bind tighter than && and ||, so they are evaluated first and logical operators combine their boolean results.
Comparisons take numbers and produce a boolean; boolean values themselves can be compared only with == and != (not <), and testing them against true is unnecessary.

x = y stores the value of y in x (a statement with a side effect); x == y only tests whether the two values are equal and gives a boolean. Writing = where == is meant is a compile error with int operands and a silent bug with boolean operands.
Used to test a numeric condition: thresholds and sign checks, range tests, divisibility (n % k == 0), loop continuation (i < N), sentinel checks, and running-extreme updates (if (x > max) max = x).

Changing < to <= (or > to >=) changes the result only at the boundary value, which in a loop guard means one more or one fewer iteration (off-by-one); mirroring the comparison (a < b to b > a) preserves the value; negating it gives the complementary operator (!(a < b) is a >= b).
rule broken: The operators are written <= and >=. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Writing =< or => (e.g. if (x => 0)).
Use comparison operators for numeric and char tests; for Strings use equals (or compareTo); for computed doubles use a tolerance; for booleans use the variable itself instead of == true.
rule broken: == compares, = assigns. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: if (a = b) with int operands (with boolean operands it compiles and silently assigns).
rule broken: == on Strings compares references, not text. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Comparing a String built at run time (input, concatenation) with a literal using ==.

sentences.c1: p && q is true only when both are true; p || q is false only when both are false.

items.text: a || b && c is evaluated left to right as (a || b) && c.
&& binds tighter than ||, so it is a || (b && c).
& and | are the same as && and || for conditions, so either can be used.
&& and || skip the right operand when the left decides the result; & and | always evaluate both, which fails when the right side depends on the left (e.g. x != 0 & y / x > 1).
A condition on several values has to be written as nested if statements, one value per if.
Several conditions combine into one boolean expression with && and ||, e.g. if (x == 0 && y == 0).
& only works on bits, so p & q cannot be used with booleans.
Java also has a & operator, which the book does not use; logical and is written &&.
Logical (boolean) operators: && (and), || (or) and ! (not), which take boolean operands and produce a boolean.
a && b is true if both operands are true and false otherwise; a || b is false if both are false and true otherwise; !a is the opposite of a; these definitions are given in full by truth tables.
! is applied before && and ||, and && before ||; the left operand is evaluated first, and for && and || the right operand is evaluated only when the left has not already decided the result.
The result is a boolean: with x = 10, x > 0 && x < 10 is false and x < 0 || x > 10 is false; true || anything is true.
The operators themselves change no variable; any side effect inside the right operand (i++, a method call) happens only if that operand is evaluated.
Combining boolean sub-expressions with &&, || and ! yields another boolean expression, so arbitrarily complex conditions can be built with parentheses.
&& and || are the short-circuit operators: in a guard such as (x != 0 && y / x > 1) the operand order matters, because the right test runs only when the left one allows it.
Comparisons bind tighter than && and ||, so comparisons are evaluated first and their boolean results are then combined (month >= 1 && month <= 12).
^ on booleans is a further logical operator, true exactly when the operands differ (it equals (a || b) && !(a && b)), but unlike && and || it always evaluates both operands.
De Morgan's laws rewrite negated && / || expressions: !(A && B) is !A || !B and !(A || B) is !A && !B.
The operands must be boolean, and the result is boolean; int operands are a compile-time error.

Used to combine several conditions into one test: a range check (lo <= x && x <= hi), alternatives (x == 0 || y == 0), a guard followed by the real test (i < n && a[i] != 0), or a rule built step by step as in LeapYear.

Swapping && for || changes the meaning; negating a whole condition requires De Morgan (negate each term and flip the operator); swapping the operands of && or || keeps the truth value but can change which side effects or exceptions occur.

Use && and || to combine conditions into a single test, ordering operands so that cheap or protective tests come first; use nested ifs only when the cases need different actions; do not use & and | for conditions.

rule broken: Conditions are combined with && and ||; & and | evaluate both operands. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: Using & or | where the right operand is only safe when the left decides first, e.g. x != 0 & y / x > 1 with x == 0 (ArithmeticException) or an out-of-range index; otherwise a silent difference only when the right side has side effects.
rule broken: && has higher precedence than ||. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Mixed && and || without parentheses intended to group the || first, e.g. a || b && c meant as (a || b) && c.

In nested loops the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer for.
print and println do the same thing, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on separate lines.
println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.
i = i++ increases i by 1.
i++ evaluates to the old value, so i = i++ stores the old value back.
i++ increases i by 2.
i++ (and ++i) increases i by exactly 1.
if (x > 0); System.out.println("positive"); prints only for positive x.
The ; ends the if with an empty statement, so the next line always runs.
println(s) prints a newline and then s.
println(s) prints s and then the newline.
System.out.println("x is 5"); sets x to 5 (text inside the quotes is run as code).
Characters inside double quotes are printed literally; println only displays them and changes no variable. Only an assignment such as x = 5; sets x.
for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times.
Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect.
x = i++ and x = ++i store the same value in x.
Both increment i, but ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.
Nested loops are a loop inside the body of another loop: the outer loop and the inner loop.
Because loops are statements, one can be the body of another; the inner loop iterates all the way through for each iteration of the outer loop.

Outer init; outer test; [inner init; inner test; inner body; inner update; ... until the inner test fails]; rest of the outer body; outer update; outer test; ... The inner init runs again on every outer pass.
The inner body runs (outer passes) x (inner passes) times: two loops of 1..10 call printf 100 times; DivisorPattern 3 prints 3 rows of 3 entries, each row ending with its row number.
One outer pass resets the inner variable, runs the complete inner loop, executes the rest of the outer body once, and then updates the outer variable once.
Usually both loops are for loops: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer for.
Matrix addition uses two nested loops over i and j; matrix multiplication adds a third, innermost loop over k for each dot product.
A plain break ends only the innermost loop; a labeled break is needed when the inner loop must end the outer one too.
Which loop is outside decides the visiting order: row index outside gives row-major order, column index outside gives column-major order.
Plan: process every pair (i, j) - two-dimensional tables, every row x column of a matrix, every pair of elements; the outer variable is a slow stepper, the inner a fast stepper.

Swapping the outer and inner loops visits the same pairs in a different order (rows vs columns), which preserves a sum but changes printed layout; moving a statement between the inner body and the outer body changes its count from (outer x inner) to outer.

Use nested loops when the work ranges over all combinations of two indices (tables, matrices, pairs); expect running time proportional to the product of the pass counts, and prefer a single loop when the second index is a function of the first.

rule broken: Without braces, the body of an if, while or for is exactly one statement; indentation does not add statements to it. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A braceless header followed by two or more indented statements: only the first is controlled, the others run once, after the if/loop, on every input.

rule broken: The inner loop needs its own loop variable. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Redeclaring the outer variable in the inner header (for (int i ...) { for (int i ...) }): 'variable i is already defined'.

rule broken: The inner loop must update its own variable. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Writing for (int j = 0; j < N; i++) in the inner loop: j never changes, so the inner loop is infinite (or i runs out of range).

17 % 5 is 3 (the quotient).

printf() ends the line like println().
printf() does not add a newline; put \n in the format string to end the line.

The number before the point is the width of the whole field; %7.2f means 7 characters in total with 2 digits after the decimal point.

9 % 5 means 9 minus 5 (a % b subtracts b from a).
% gives the remainder after integer division: 9 % 5 is 4 because 9 = 1 * 5 + 4, and 17 % 5 is 2, not 12.
Loop statement: `do { body } while (cond);` is a loop whose test comes after the body, so the body runs one or more times.

`do { <statements> } while (<boolean expression>);` (note the final semicolon) means the same as the corresponding while loop except that the first test of the condition is omitted. (Spec: JLS §14.13.)
Order: execute the body; evaluate the condition; if true, execute the body again and re-test; stop the first time the condition is false at the bottom test.
do-while produces no value. Its result is the state after the last pass. In the unit-disk example, x and y end inside the disk after about 4/π ≈ 1.27 passes on average.

One pass runs every statement of the body once (e.g. new random x and y) and then evaluates the condition, a boolean that decides whether another pass follows. The test changes nothing unless it has side effects.
do { S } while (c); equals `S; while (c) { S }`. If c is initially true it behaves exactly like `while (c) { S }`; if c is initially false it still runs S once where the while runs it zero times.

Nested loops are a loop inside the body of another loop: the outer loop and the inner loop.
Because loops are statements, one can be the body of another; the inner loop iterates all the way through for each iteration of the outer loop.

Outer init; outer test; [inner init; inner test; inner body; inner update; ... until the inner test fails]; rest of the outer body; outer update; outer test; ... The inner init runs again on every outer pass.
The inner body runs (outer passes) x (inner passes) times: two loops of 1..10 call printf 100 times; DivisorPattern 3 prints 3 rows of 3 entries, each row ending with its row number.
One outer pass resets the inner variable, runs the complete inner loop, executes the rest of the outer body once, and then updates the outer variable once.
Usually both loops are for loops: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer for.
Matrix addition uses two nested loops over i and j; matrix multiplication adds a third, innermost loop over k for each dot product.
A plain break ends only the innermost loop; a labeled break is needed when the inner loop must end the outer one too.
Which loop is outside decides the visiting order: row index outside gives row-major order, column index outside gives column-major order.
Plan: process every pair (i, j) - two-dimensional tables, every row x column of a matrix, every pair of elements; the outer variable is a slow stepper, the inner a fast stepper.

Swapping the outer and inner loops visits the same pairs in a different order (rows vs columns), which preserves a sum but changes printed layout; moving a statement between the inner body and the outer body changes its count from (outer x inner) to outer.

Use nested loops when the work ranges over all combinations of two indices (tables, matrices, pairs); expect running time proportional to the product of the pass counts, and prefer a single loop when the second index is a function of the first.

items.text: Remainder operator %: the binary operator that gives the remainder after dividing a by b.
For ints, a % b is defined so that (a / b) * b + a % b equals a. The result takes the sign of a, % by zero throws ArithmeticException, and % also works on doubles.
Evaluate a, then b, take the quotient rounded toward 0, and give what is left over. % has the same precedence as * and /, and they group left to right.
r = a % b stores a remainder smaller in size than b and leaves a and b unchanged. If b is 0, ArithmeticException is thrown before anything is stored.
% is the companion of integer division, since a == (a / b) * b + a % b. Both use the same quotient rounded toward 0.
Plans: divisibility and parity tests (x % 2 == 0), digit extraction (x % 10), cyclic wrap-around ((i + 1) % n), leap-year rules, and splitting units (76 % 12 inches).

Negating a flips the remainder's sign, so n % 2 == 1 fails for negative odd n while n % 2 != 0 still works. Changing the divisor changes the cycle length. Swapping % with / swaps the remainder for the quotient.

Use % for divisibility, parity, digits, cyclic indices and unit splitting. Do not use it for percentages (use * / 100.0), and do not use it where a non-negative mathematical mod is needed for negative values (adjust the result or use Math.floorMod).
rule broken: int remainder by zero is undefined. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: x % 0, or a divisor variable that is 0: ArithmeticException: / by zero.

rule broken: The remainder takes the sign of the dividend. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Negative inputs in an odd test written as x % 2 == 1, or in a wrap-around index computed as (i - 1) % n.
rule broken: % is the remainder, not a percentage. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Writing price % 15 for 15 percent of price.

items.text: Each case of a switch normally ends with break, which exits the switch body.
After the matching case runs, the switch ends even without break.
Without break, statements in switch blocks fall through into the following cases.
break ends the whole program.
break ends only the innermost loop (or switch); execution continues after it.
break leaves the if statement it is written in.
break immediately exits a loop without letting it run to completion, and in a switch it exits the switch body.
break has no effect; the loop body just carries on.
break leaves the innermost loop at once; the rest of the body and later passes do not run.
break starts the next iteration of the loop.
break exits the loop immediately; continue skips to the next iteration of the loop.
Selection statement: `switch (expr) { case v1: ...; break; ... default: ... }` chooses among many alternatives by the value of one expression.

The selector is an int-like (char, byte, short, int), String or enum expression. Case labels are distinct constants of that type, and default is optional. Control jumps to the matching label (or to default, or past the switch), and the case statements usually end with break. Without a break, execution falls through into the statements of the next case; default runs when no case matches.

Order: evaluate the selector once; compare it with the case constants; jump to the matching label (else default, else skip the switch). Then execute the statements from there in order, through later labels, until a break or the closing brace.
A switch statement has no value. Its result is the effect of the case(s) run: with `day = 3`, the S&W day switch prints Wed. Without breaks, day = 5 would print Fri, then Sat.
One execution evaluates the selector once (any side effect in it happens once) and runs the statements of one entry point and any cases it falls into. It changes only what those statements change.
A switch replaces an if-else chain only when every test is `expr == constant` on the same expression. Range tests such as the income-bracket chain (`income < 47450`) must stay an if-else chain.
Each case is normally ended by break, which exits the switch body. Leaving it out makes that case fall into the next. Inside a loop, that break exits the switch, not the loop.

Plan: multiway dispatch or lookup. It maps one discrete value (day number, menu choice, character) to one of several actions or results. Grouped labels (`case "apple": case "banana":`) map several values to one action.

When every case ends with break, reordering the cases does not change behaviour (labels are distinct constants). Removing one break changes behaviour for that value only. Adding a default changes only values with no matching label.

Use switch for more than two mutually exclusive alternatives decided by equality of one int, char, String or enum value. Use an if-else chain for ranges, doubles or unrelated conditions. Use an array lookup (S&W 1.4) when each case only selects a value.

rule broken: Without break, execution falls through into the following cases. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Any selector value whose case lacks a break: the following cases' statements also run (e.g. both Fri and Sat printed).

rule broken: Values that match no case do nothing unless a default is present. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: An out-of-range selector (day = 7) with no default: nothing happens, and a variable assigned only in the cases may stay unassigned.

rule broken: Case labels must be distinct compile-time constants of the selector type, and the selector may not be double, float, long or boolean. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Duplicate `case 1:` labels, a variable as a label, or `switch (x)` with x a double.
rule broken: A String selector is dereferenced. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: Switching on a String variable that is null throws NullPointerException.

printf is the formatted-print method of standard output. It takes a format string and arguments and writes the formatted string.

items.text: ++ and -- are the increment and decrement operators: shorthand that adds 1 to (or subtracts 1 from) a numeric variable.
++ has the same effect as i = i + 1 and -- the same as i = i - 1; as statements i++ and ++i are the same, but in expressions ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.

i++: fetch the value of i (that is the expression's value), then store i + 1 into i. ++i: store i + 1 into i, and the new value is the expression's value. Both happen before the rest of the enclosing expression continues.
With i = 5: x = i++ gives x = 5, i = 6; x = ++i gives x = 6, i = 6; i = i++ leaves i = 5.
One execution changes exactly one variable (i) by exactly 1 and returns its old (i++) or new (++i) value.
The usual for-loop update is i++ (shorthand for i = i + 1); as a stand-alone update statement ++i and i++ give the same loop.
Inside a larger expression the result depends on which value (old or new) the increment yields and on left-to-right evaluation, e.g. j += j++ in Exercise 1.3.6.
i++ is shorthand for the assignment i = i + 1 (and i += k for i = i + k), so it changes the variable's stored value.
i++, ++i and i += 1 all add 1 to i; ++ and -- change a variable only by one and are normally used for integers, while i += k works for any amount and with any arithmetic operator (-=, *=, /=, %=).
Plan/role: the update of a stepper or counter (count++ in a counter, i++ in a counted loop).
As a stand-alone statement, replacing i++ by ++i, i += 1 or i = i + 1 preserves behaviour; inside an expression (x = i++ vs x = ++i) the swap changes the value used by 1.
Use i++ / i-- as stand-alone statements and in for-loop updates; avoid them inside larger expressions (x = ++i), as the book does, and use += for steps other than 1.

rule broken: ++ and -- apply only to a variable. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Applying ++ to a value that is not a variable, e.g. 5++ or (i + 1)++: compile-time error.

items.text: A short simulation gives the exact page ranks.

The page ranks depend on which page the surfer starts from.
For the random-surfer chain the long-run probabilities do not depend on the starting page.

A program does not produce accurate answers simply because it can print numbers to many decimal places of precision; ensuring accuracy is often the most difficult challenge.
A mathematical model: a random process on states (pages) whose moves are given by a transition matrix.
The surfer's random process is a Markov chain; by the basic limit theorem the probability of eventually ending on any page is the same for all starting pages (mixing), though not all chains mix.
State sequence: from the current page i, choose the next page j with probability p[i][j]; repeat from j. In probability form, the t-step distribution is the (t-1)-step distribution times the matrix.
Produces the stationary probabilities (page ranks): for tiny.txt about .27 .27 .15 .25 .07.
One step moves the state from page i to a page j drawn from row i; in matrix form, one multiplication turns the distribution after t-1 moves into the distribution after t moves.
The chain is defined by the matrix: it must be square with every row a probability distribution.
Each vector-matrix multiplication advances the chain's probabilities by one move; repeating it approaches the stationary vector.
Model a memoryless random process to compute its long-run behaviour (page ranks) instead of following one surfer.
Changing the start state keeps the limiting distribution (if the chain mixes); removing the random leap can break mixing; squaring the matrix gives two-step probabilities.

Right model when the next state depends only on the current state with fixed probabilities (web surfing, many random processes); its limit theorem gives start-independent results only for chains that mix.

items.text: Nested loops are a loop inside the body of another loop: the outer loop and the inner loop.
Because loops are statements, one can be the body of another; the inner loop iterates all the way through for each iteration of the outer loop.

Outer init; outer test; [inner init; inner test; inner body; inner update; ... until the inner test fails]; rest of the outer body; outer update; outer test; ... The inner init runs again on every outer pass.
The inner body runs (outer passes) x (inner passes) times: two loops of 1..10 call printf 100 times; DivisorPattern 3 prints 3 rows of 3 entries, each row ending with its row number.
One outer pass resets the inner variable, runs the complete inner loop, executes the rest of the outer body once, and then updates the outer variable once.
Usually both loops are for loops: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer for.
Matrix addition uses two nested loops over i and j; matrix multiplication adds a third, innermost loop over k for each dot product.
A plain break ends only the innermost loop; a labeled break is needed when the inner loop must end the outer one too.
Which loop is outside decides the visiting order: row index outside gives row-major order, column index outside gives column-major order.
Plan: process every pair (i, j) - two-dimensional tables, every row x column of a matrix, every pair of elements; the outer variable is a slow stepper, the inner a fast stepper.

Swapping the outer and inner loops visits the same pairs in a different order (rows vs columns), which preserves a sum but changes printed layout; moving a statement between the inner body and the outer body changes its count from (outer x inner) to outer.

Use nested loops when the work ranges over all combinations of two indices (tables, matrices, pairs); expect running time proportional to the product of the pass counts, and prefer a single loop when the second index is a function of the first.

rule broken: The inner loop must update its own variable. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Writing for (int j = 0; j < N; i++) in the inner loop: j never changes, so the inner loop is infinite (or i runs out of range).

Nested loops are a loop inside the body of another loop: the outer loop and the inner loop.
Because loops are statements, one can be the body of another; the inner loop iterates all the way through for each iteration of the outer loop.

Outer init; outer test; [inner init; inner test; inner body; inner update; ... until the inner test fails]; rest of the outer body; outer update; outer test; ... The inner init runs again on every outer pass.
The inner body runs (outer passes) x (inner passes) times: two loops of 1..10 call printf 100 times; DivisorPattern 3 prints 3 rows of 3 entries, each row ending with its row number.
One outer pass resets the inner variable, runs the complete inner loop, executes the rest of the outer body once, and then updates the outer variable once.
Usually both loops are for loops: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer for.
Matrix addition uses two nested loops over i and j; matrix multiplication adds a third, innermost loop over k for each dot product.
A plain break ends only the innermost loop; a labeled break is needed when the inner loop must end the outer one too.
Which loop is outside decides the visiting order: row index outside gives row-major order, column index outside gives column-major order.
Plan: process every pair (i, j) - two-dimensional tables, every row x column of a matrix, every pair of elements; the outer variable is a slow stepper, the inner a fast stepper.

Swapping the outer and inner loops visits the same pairs in a different order (rows vs columns), which preserves a sum but changes printed layout; moving a statement between the inner body and the outer body changes its count from (outer x inner) to outer.

Use nested loops when the work ranges over all combinations of two indices (tables, matrices, pairs); expect running time proportional to the product of the pass counts, and prefer a single loop when the second index is a function of the first.

rule broken: The inner loop must update its own variable. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Writing for (int j = 0; j < N; i++) in the inner loop: j never changes, so the inner loop is infinite (or i runs out of range).

double is a primitive data type: Java's 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point type for representing real numbers.

Values are 64-bit IEEE 754 numbers (about 15 significant digits) plus the special values Infinity and NaN; +, -, *, / (and %) are defined; if at least one operand of a binary arithmetic operator is double, the operation is a floating-point operation.

Operators are applied in precedence order, left operand first; at each operator, if one operand is double the other is widened to double before the operation, and the result is rounded to the nearest double before the next operator uses it.
The result has type double: 5.0/3.0 is 1.6666666666666667, 10/3.0 is 3.3333333333333335, 1.0/0.0 is Infinity, Math.sqrt(-1.0) is NaN; println always shows a decimal part (3.0, not 3).

An assignment to a double variable stores the nearest representable value (x = x + 0.1 replaces x with the rounded sum); no double operation throws an exception, so the variable may end up holding Infinity or NaN.

Type flow decides the division: with two int operands a / b discards the fraction (10/3 is 3, and double d = 10/3; stores 3.0); if either operand is double the other is promoted and the fraction is kept (10/3.0 is 3.3333333333333335).
double and boolean never convert into each other (no cast is allowed either way); they meet only through comparisons, which take doubles and produce a boolean, e.g. (x < 3.1).
char is an integral numeric type, so a char widens automatically to double in arithmetic ('a' + 0.5 is 97.5), but a double needs an explicit cast to become a char.
Every double operation rounds its result to the nearest representable value, so double results carry rounding error that can accumulate; this is why == on computed doubles is unreliable.
For double operands a zero divisor is not an error: 1.0/0.0 is Infinity, -1.0/0.0 is -Infinity and 0.0/0.0 is NaN, whereas int division by zero throws an exception.
double is one of the eight primitive types and the default type of decimal literals (float would need an f suffix and is not used in the book).
Used for measured or computed real quantities (physics formulas, roots, averages, probabilities); a double variable often plays the gatherer role, as in Harmonic's sum += 1.0/i.

Changing a variable from int to double changes / from truncating to real division and changes the printed form (3 becomes 3.0); changing back needs a cast and loses the fraction. Invariant: values are approximations, so reordering a sum ((a+b)+c vs a+(b+c)) may change the last digits.

Use double for real-valued quantities where approximate results are acceptable (science, geometry, probabilities, averages); do not use it for counts, array indices, loop counters or money that must be exact (use int or long, e.g. cents).

Running (executing) a program is launching it with java Name so that the Java Virtual Machine follows its instructions.

The development cycle is the same in any environment (terminal or IDE): edit the .java file, compile it with javac, run it with java.

Definite assignment: the compile-time rule that a local variable must certainly have been assigned before any read of it.

Every access of a local variable must be preceded by an assignment on every possible path, or the program does not compile. The analysis ignores run-time values, except for constant booleans and the operators && || ?:.

The compiler walks the control flow. After a declaration with no initializer the variable is unassigned, and an assignment makes it assigned on that path. Where paths merge (after if/else) it counts as assigned only if every incoming path assigned it, and an assignment inside a while body does not count after the loop.
The result appears at compile time: the code either compiles or reports 'variable x might not have been initialized'. No default value is ever produced for a local variable.
The first assignment (initialization) moves a variable from unassigned to holding a value, and only then may it be read.
A declaration without an initializer leaves the local unassigned. Writing = value in the declaration satisfies the rule at once.

A local variable has no value until it is assigned: using it first is a compile-time error. An array element is given a default value (0, 0.0, false) when the array is created with new, so it can be read before any assignment.

The rule guarantees that no program reads a meaningless value. The matching plan is to initialize counters and accumulators before the loop that updates them (int sum = 0; then sum += i inside the loop).

Moving an initialization into one branch of an if, or into a loop body, breaks compilation of the reads that follow. Adding an else branch that also assigns, or initializing at the declaration, restores it.

Initialize at the declaration whenever a sensible first value exists (0 for counters and sums). Leave the declaration bare only when every branch that follows assigns it. The rule covers local variables only: array elements and fields get default values.

items.text: Arithmetic operators: the binary operators + - * / % that combine two numeric operands into a numeric result.

Both operands must be numeric, and the result has the promoted type (int, long or double). * / % bind tighter than + -, all group left to right, and int / or % by zero throws ArithmeticException. Unary minus negates its operand (-x) and unary plus leaves it unchanged; they bind more tightly than * and /, so -a * b is (-a) * b.
The left operand is evaluated fully, then the right operand, and then the operator is applied in the promoted type.
With ints, 17 / 3 is 5 and 17 % 3 is 2. With doubles, 5.0 / 3.0 is 1.6666666666666667. With mixed operands, the int is promoted first (10 / 3.0 is 3.333...).
An arithmetic operator never changes its operands. Each variable is replaced by its value, and only an assignment (or ++ or op=) stores the result.
Operators build larger expressions from smaller ones, and each operand can itself be any expression.
For ints, / gives the truncated quotient and % the remainder, so (a / b) * b + a % b == a.
int / or % by zero throws a run-time exception, while floating-point division by zero gives Infinity or NaN.

+ adds when both operands are numbers and concatenates when either operand is a String, converting the other operand to a String. It is left-associative, so 1 + 2 + "3" is "33" but "1" + 2 + 3 is "123".
Arithmetic operators turn formulas into code: totals, averages, unit conversions (inch * CM_PER_INCH), and digit extraction (n % 10, n / 10).

Changing an operand's type changes the operator's meaning (int / versus double /). Reordering * and / changes integer results (59 * 100 / 60 is 98, 59 / 60 * 100 is 0). Replacing ^ with Math.pow gives a real power.
Use the operators for arithmetic on numeric types. Use the Math library for powers, roots and absolute values, and parse numeric Strings before computing with them.

Arithmetic operators: the binary operators + - * / % that combine two numeric operands into a numeric result.

Both operands must be numeric, and the result has the promoted type (int, long or double). * / % bind tighter than + -, all group left to right, and int / or % by zero throws ArithmeticException. Unary minus negates its operand (-x) and unary plus leaves it unchanged; they bind more tightly than * and /, so -a * b is (-a) * b.
The left operand is evaluated fully, then the right operand, and then the operator is applied in the promoted type.
With ints, 17 / 3 is 5 and 17 % 3 is 2. With doubles, 5.0 / 3.0 is 1.6666666666666667. With mixed operands, the int is promoted first (10 / 3.0 is 3.333...).
An arithmetic operator never changes its operands. Each variable is replaced by its value, and only an assignment (or ++ or op=) stores the result.
Operators build larger expressions from smaller ones, and each operand can itself be any expression.
For ints, / gives the truncated quotient and % the remainder, so (a / b) * b + a % b == a.
int / or % by zero throws a run-time exception, while floating-point division by zero gives Infinity or NaN.

+ adds when both operands are numbers and concatenates when either operand is a String, converting the other operand to a String. It is left-associative, so 1 + 2 + "3" is "33" but "1" + 2 + 3 is "123".
Arithmetic operators turn formulas into code: totals, averages, unit conversions (inch * CM_PER_INCH), and digit extraction (n % 10, n / 10).

++ and -- are the increment and decrement operators: shorthand that adds 1 to (or subtracts 1 from) a numeric variable.

Which branch runs is decided by what the programmer meant or by code outside the if, not by whether the condition is true.
The then branch runs exactly when the condition evaluates to true at the moment it is tested; otherwise the else branch (if any) runs.
Writes the same statements in both branches of an if-else.
Code common to both branches belongs before or after the if-else.
The else branch of an if-else statement always executes.
The else branch runs only when the if condition is false.
if (c) A else B is the same as if (c) A followed by if (!c) B.
In if-else, c is tested once and exactly one of A or B runs, even if A changes the variables that c uses.
System.out.println is a library method that prints its argument followed by a line terminator ('print line').
println(String x) behaves as though it calls print(x) and then println(); println() terminates the current line by writing the line separator string.
Evaluate the argument, print its characters at the current position, then write the line separator so the cursor moves to the beginning of the next line.
Output is the value's characters followed by a line break: println("Hello, "); println("World!"); prints two lines.
One call appends the text and a line separator to the output; the cursor ends at the start of the next line; no variable changes and nothing is returned.
System.out.println(s); is a statement, so its line of output appears at its own place in the sequence.
println("s") outputs exactly the characters between the quotes and then ends the line.
print leaves the cursor on the line; println ends it; several prints followed by one println make one line.
println prints numbers with all their digits and always ends the line; printf formats each value by its conversion code and ends the line only where the format has %n or \n.
Purpose: produce one complete line of output, e.g. each result on its own line, or end a line built with print.
Replacing println with print joins the next output onto the same line (a typical logic error); the characters printed stay the same.
Use println when each output item belongs on its own line or to end a line; use print to continue a line and printf to control number formatting.
rule broken: Finish a line of print calls with println. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: output ends with print, so the last line may not be shown or runs into the shell prompt
rule broken: Method names are case-sensitive. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: System.out.Println or system.out.println: cannot find symbol
rule broken: Calls need parentheses. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: System.out.println; without ()

question: Which variable is an accumulator and which is a counter?
answer: sum builds a total, count counts.

sentences.c1: sum builds a total, count counts.

items.text: i++, ++i and i += 1 all add 1 to i; ++ and -- change a variable only by one and are normally used for integers, while i += k works for any amount and with any arithmetic operator (-=, *=, /=, %=).
Updates the loop counter so that the loop runs the wrong number of times.
The init, test and update together decide the number of passes; trace them to check the count.
The repeat count of a counted loop says how many of the body statements are executed.
The repeat count is how many times the whole body runs; every pass runs all body statements.
X[i] names the whole array, not one element.
The array is a; a[i] is the single element at index i.
x = i++ and x = ++i store the same value in x.
Both increment i, but ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.
i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value.
i is a position; a[i] is the value stored at that position.
The first element of a is a[1].
Numbering begins with 0; the first element is a[0].
if (x > 0); System.out.println("positive"); prints only for positive x.
The ; ends the if with an empty statement, so the next line always runs.
= compares two values instead of assigning
x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
++ and -- are the increment and decrement operators: shorthand that adds 1 to (or subtracts 1 from) a numeric variable.
++ has the same effect as i = i + 1 and -- the same as i = i - 1; as statements i++ and ++i are the same, but in expressions ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.

i++: fetch the value of i (that is the expression's value), then store i + 1 into i. ++i: store i + 1 into i, and the new value is the expression's value. Both happen before the rest of the enclosing expression continues.
With i = 5: x = i++ gives x = 5, i = 6; x = ++i gives x = 6, i = 6; i = i++ leaves i = 5.
One execution changes exactly one variable (i) by exactly 1 and returns its old (i++) or new (++i) value.
The usual for-loop update is i++ (shorthand for i = i + 1); as a stand-alone update statement ++i and i++ give the same loop.
Inside a larger expression the result depends on which value (old or new) the increment yields and on left-to-right evaluation, e.g. j += j++ in Exercise 1.3.6.
i++ is shorthand for the assignment i = i + 1 (and i += k for i = i + k), so it changes the variable's stored value.
i++, ++i and i += 1 all add 1 to i; ++ and -- change a variable only by one and are normally used for integers, while i += k works for any amount and with any arithmetic operator (-=, *=, /=, %=).
Plan/role: the update of a stepper or counter (count++ in a counter, i++ in a counted loop).
As a stand-alone statement, replacing i++ by ++i, i += 1 or i = i + 1 preserves behaviour; inside an expression (x = i++ vs x = ++i) the swap changes the value used by 1.
Use i++ / i-- as stand-alone statements and in for-loop updates; avoid them inside larger expressions (x = ++i), as the book does, and use += for steps other than 1.
rule broken: i = i++ stores the old value back. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Writing i = i++ to increment: i never changes, so a loop driven by it is infinite.
rule broken: ++ and -- apply only to a variable. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Applying ++ to a value that is not a variable, e.g. 5++ or (i + 1)++: compile-time error.

question: A classmate always gets 0.0. Their test is  (int) Math.random() * 6 + 1 == 6.  Find the cause by reasoning.
answer: The cast happens first, so (int) Math.random() is 0 and the die is always 1. Cast after multiplying.

sentences.c2: so (int) Math.random() is 0 and the die is always 1.

items.text: To turn Math.random()'s double in [0, 1) into a random int from 0 to N-1, multiply it by N and cast the result to int.
Math.random() can return exactly 1.0.
Math.random() returns a value in [0, 1): 0 is possible, 1 is not.
(double) (3 / 5) is 0.6.
The integer division 3 / 5 = 0 happens before the cast, so the result is 0.0.
Changing a later literal to 100.0 fixes an earlier int division.
The int division happens first; the double must be in the division itself.
Writes int n = Math.round(x); because Math.round gives an int.
Math.round(double) returns a long, so storing it in an int needs a cast: int n = (int) Math.round(x);
(int) 2.7 evaluates to 3.
A cast to int discards the fractional part (rounds toward zero, so (int) -2.7 is -2); Math.round rounds to the nearest integer.
(int) 2.5 / 0.15 casts the whole quotient to int.
The cast applies only to what comes right after it, here 2.5.
(int) args[0] converts the text "34" into the number 34.
A String argument that represents a number must be converted with a method such as Integer.parseInt.
An int result that is too large is automatically stored as a bigger number.
int arithmetic is 32-bit; a result outside the range wraps around.
A cast is a unary operator, written (type) expression, that converts a value of one primitive type to another, used when the conversion may lose information.

(T) e converts the value of e to type T; a double-to-int cast discards the fraction by rounding toward zero; a cast is required for narrowing conversions; it has higher precedence than arithmetic; casts between boolean and numbers, or from String to int, are not allowed.
Evaluate the operand immediately to the right of the cast (a parenthesized expression is evaluated completely first), convert that value, then continue with the remaining operators of the expression.
(int) 2.71828 is int 2; (int) -2.7 is -2; (int) 11 * 0.3 is double 3.3; (int) (11 * 0.3) is int 3; (double) 3 / 5 is 0.6 but (double) (3 / 5) is 0.0; (char) ('a' + 4) is 'e'.
A cast yields a new value and changes nothing else: neither the type nor the value of the variable being cast changes (after int x = (int) pi; pi is still 3.14159).
A cast is the explicit conversion between primitive types, needed exactly where automatic conversion is refused because information may be lost.
To turn Math.random()'s double into a random int from 0 to N-1, the cast must enclose the product: (int) (Math.random() * N); casting first gives 0.
x op= e contains an implicit cast back to the type of x, so with int x, x += 0.5 compiles (x = (int) (x + 0.5)) while x = x + 0.5 is a compile-time error.

Widening (promotion) happens automatically when a value goes to a type with a larger range (int to double) and loses nothing; a narrowing conversion (double to int) is never automatic and needs an explicit cast, which truncates toward zero.
(int) 2.71828 truncates toward zero and gives 2; Math.round(2.71828) rounds to the nearest integer and gives 3, as a long that needs (int) to become an int.

Used to discard information on purpose: truncating a scaled random number to an index, taking the integer part, converting between char and int codes ((char) ('a' + k)), or forcing real division with (double) sum / n.

Moving the parentheses changes when truncation happens ((int) (a * b) vs (int) a * b); removing a cast from a narrowing assignment turns it into a compile-time error; int to double to int restores the value, but double to int to double loses the fraction.

Use a cast when you intend to truncate or narrow (random indices, integer parts, char codes); use Math.round to round, Integer.parseInt for Strings, and put a double into the division itself rather than casting its int result.
rule broken: Math.round(double) returns a long, so storing it in an int needs a cast: int n = (int) Math.round(x);. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: int n = Math.round(x); with double x.

rule broken: A cast applies only to the value right after it. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: int n = (int) 11 * 0.3; the product is still a double (possible loss of precision); in a double context the same mistake is a silent logic error ((int) pi * 20.0 gives 60.0).
rule broken: Casts require compatible types. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: (int) "3" or (int) args[0] on a String, or a cast between boolean and a number.

question: How do break and continue differ in the first loop?
answer: continue jumps to the next i for the even numbers, break stops the loop completely at 5.

sentences.c1: continue jumps to the next i for the even numbers, break stops the loop completely at 5.

items.text: break ends the whole loop; continue ends only the current pass.
break starts the next iteration of the loop.
break exits the loop immediately; continue skips to the next iteration of the loop.
break ends the whole program.
break ends only the innermost loop (or switch); execution continues after it.
continue ends the loop.
continue skips the rest of the current pass: control transfers directly to the increment statement for the next iteration of the loop.
break has no effect; the loop body just carries on.
break leaves the innermost loop at once; the rest of the body and later passes do not run.
continue means carry on with the rest of the loop body, so it has no effect.
continue skips the rest of the current iteration.
break leaves the if statement it is written in.
break immediately exits a loop without letting it run to completion, and in a switch it exits the switch body.
Jump statement: `break;` immediately ends the innermost enclosing while, for, do or switch.
`break;` may appear only inside a loop or switch. When executed, it completes that innermost loop or switch at once, and control passes to the statement after it. (Spec: JLS §14.15.)

When `break` executes: the remaining statements of the body are skipped, the for-loop increment and the condition are not evaluated again, and control continues at the first statement after the loop. In `for (i = 2; i <= N/i; i++) if (N % i == 0) break;` it runs right after the test that found a divisor.

break is a statement and produces no value. Its effect shows in the variables it leaves: after the primality loop for N = 15, i is 3 (the smallest divisor), so `i > N/i` is false and 'is prime' is not printed.
One execution of break changes no variable. It changes only the point of control (to after the loop), so every variable keeps its value at the moment of the break.

break gives a while loop a second exit, in the middle of the body. After the loop, the program has to tell which exit was taken by re-testing the state (as in `if (i > N/i)`), so any variable used for that test must be declared before the loop.
Plain break reaches only the innermost loop. In nested loops, ending the outer loop needs `break label;` on a labeled outer statement (or a flag tested by the outer loop).
Both skip the rest of the current body. break then leaves the loop (no increment, no further test); continue goes on to the increment and the next test.
In a switch, break ends the switch body; without it, execution falls through into the next case. A break inside a switch that is inside a loop exits only the switch, not the loop.

Two ways to stop a search when the item is found: break leaves the loop at once, while a boolean flag is set and tested in the loop condition so the loop ends at its next test. After either, the code must tell the found case from the loop finishing normally.

Plan: early-exit search (Soloway 'loop-and-a-half' or exit-on-found). Stop scanning as soon as the answer is known, e.g. at the first divisor; the loop variable is a stepper whose value at exit reports the find.

Removing the break keeps the loop finite but lets it run to completion. In the prime test, i then ends above N/i for every N, so composites are reported as prime. Invariant kept with break: after the loop, `i <= N/i` holds exactly when the break was taken.

Use break when the reason to stop is discovered in the middle of a pass (first divisor, sentinel found) and folding it into the loop condition would be awkward. Prefer a plain loop condition when the exit can be stated up front. In a method, `return` is often clearer. S&W use break rarely.
rule broken: break must be inside a loop or switch. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: `break;` inside an if that is not inside any loop or switch (break outside switch or loop).
rule broken: Statements after break in the same block can never run. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Code written directly after `break;` in the same block (unreachable statement).

rule broken: break exits only the innermost loop or switch. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A break in an inner loop (or in a switch inside a loop) that was meant to end the outer loop: the outer loop keeps going.

question: What is an infinite loop?
answer: A loop that never stops because its condition stays true.

items.text: A while tests its boolean condition before every pass and stops the first time it evaluates to false.
A comparison such as x < y produces a boolean result; comparisons together with boolean logic provide the basis for decision-making.
A while loop runs its body once when the condition is true, just like an if.
A while tests its condition again after every pass and keeps repeating while the condition stays true.
A while loop ends by itself even if nothing in the body changes the variable tested in the condition.
If no statement in the body changes a variable in the condition, a condition that was true stays true and the loop never ends.
For and while loops end when the condition becomes true.
A for or while loop ends when its condition becomes false.
Writes else (x > 0) with a condition but no if.
else takes no condition; use else if (x > 0).
a condition that never goes false still terminates
A while loop stops only when its condition is false at a check, so if no pass changes the variables in the condition, it never stops.
A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats.
Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.
A true/false question is answered with arithmetic (e.g. 1 for true).
A logic question is written as a boolean expression whose value is true or false.
To get a boolean from x > y you need ok = (x > y) ? true : false;.
ok = (x > y); already gives the boolean, so the ? : is unnecessary.
Loop bug/behaviour: a loop whose continuation condition never becomes false, so it runs until the program is killed (or overflow intervenes).
A while or for loop terminates only if some pass makes its condition false at a test (or a break or return runs). Otherwise it repeats forever. The compiler does not check this.
The same order as any loop: test, body, test... In an infinite loop the update either never runs or never moves the tested variables towards false, so every test yields true.

There is no final value. Either output scrolls forever (BadHellos with `i > 3`) or nothing happens and the program 'hangs'. Over a very long run, int overflow may eventually make the test false (BadHellos stops after about 2^31 lines).
Each pass leaves the condition's variables either unchanged or moving away from false (i grows while the test is `i > 3`). So the state after the pass satisfies the condition again.

A loop is finite only if its update moves the control variable towards making the condition false. Wrong direction (`i--` with `i < n`), wrong step (`i += 0` or `x += 0.5` on an int), or a condition that the update can step over (`i != 10` with `i += 3`) all give infinite loops.
Purpose: usually a bug. An intentional `while (true)` with an internal break or return is the 'loop-and-a-half' plan for servers, event loops and read-until-sentinel input.

Changing the condition or update can turn a terminating loop into an infinite one (`i <= 10` to `i > 3`), or the reverse. The termination argument (a quantity that strictly moves towards the bound on every pass) must survive any change.

Write `while (true)` only when the exit is in the middle of the body and is certain (break or return on a sentinel or event). Otherwise, for each loop, state why the condition eventually becomes false. When a program seems stuck, add trace prints to tell an infinite loop from a slow one.

rule broken: The body must change a variable in the condition so that it eventually becomes false. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A forgotten `i++` (or an update inside an if or after a continue): the program hangs or prints forever.
rule broken: An empty statement after the loop header becomes the body. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: `while (i < 10); { i++; }`: the stray `;` is an empty body that never changes i.

rule broken: Tests on doubles or on exact values can be stepped over. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: `for (double x = 0.0; x != 1.0; x += 0.1)` or `while (i != 10) i += 3;`: the variable jumps past the stopping value.

rule broken: int arithmetic wraps without warning. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: `for (int i = 0; i <= Integer.MAX_VALUE; i++)`: i overflows to a negative value, so the test is never false.
rule broken: Code after a loop that can never complete normally is unreachable. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Statements after `while (true) { ... }` with no break (unreachable statement).

question: Why can a[0] be printed when a local  int x;  without a value cannot?
answer: new fills the array with 0s, but a local variable has no value until you give it one.

sentences.c2: but a local variable has no value until you give it one.

items.text: An array must be created with new before any of its elements a[i] can be accessed.
int x; inside main starts at 0, so x can be used before anything is assigned to it.
A local variable has no value until it is assigned, and using it before then does not compile.
An array cannot have length 0.
new int[0] is a legal array of length 0.
new int[n] has slots 0 to n, inclusive.
The slots are 0 to n - 1.
new int[n] with a negative n creates an empty array.
Creating an array with a negative length throws NegativeArraySizeException at run time.
Arrays are created without the new keyword.
An array is created with new (or with an initializer list in a declaration).
A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global.
A local variable exists only from its declaration to the end of its block.
A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model).
Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.
A variable can contain more than one value.
A variable holds exactly one value at a time; assigning a new value replaces the old one.
Identity: an array creation expression; new T[n] makes a new array object with n elements of type T and yields a reference to it.
Declarative: 'new T[expr]', where expr is any int-valued expression evaluated at run time; the resulting length is fixed for the array's lifetime.

Sequencing: (1) the dimension expression is evaluated; (2) if it is negative, NegativeArraySizeException is thrown; (3) space for n elements is reserved and every element is set to its default; (4) the expression yields the reference, which an enclosing assignment then stores.

Result: a value of type T[], namely a reference to a new array of length n whose elements all hold the default (0, 0.0, false or null). It produces no output; printing it shows an address, not the elements.
State transition: one execution creates one new array object (n new element variables at their defaults) and returns its reference. No existing variable changes until that reference is assigned.
The declared element type must match the created one; in 'double[] a = new double[N];' the left side is the declaration and the right side is the creation.
Elements can be indexed only after creation, and the n given to new fixes the valid index range 0..n-1.
Creation is what puts the default value (0, 0.0, false, null) in every slot; each execution of new gives fresh defaults.
The size n given to new becomes a.length and never changes for that array object.
An initializer {v0, ..., vk} implies creation of an array of length k+1, so new is not written.
Only new makes a distinct array. Assignment copies the reference, so a separate copy needs new plus an element-by-element copy.
new yields the reference (address) of the array, and the array variable stores that reference, not the elements.
Plan/role: reserve storage for a number of values that may be known only at run time (e.g. N from the command line), before any value is stored.

Conservation: changing n changes a.length and the valid index range but not the element type. Moving 'new' inside a loop gives a fresh array of defaults on every pass (SelfAvoidingWalk relies on this). Re-creating an array never changes arrays that other variables already refer to.

rule broken: The dimension expression of new must be >= 0. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: the size evaluates to a negative int, e.g. a negative command-line value, or int overflow such as new int[N*N*N*N] with N = 1000 (NegativeArraySizeException)

Applicability: use new T[n] when the number of values is known (at least at run time) before they are stored and stays fixed. Use an initializer when the values are compile-time constants, and a resizing structure when the count is unknown in advance.

question: What does  System.out.println(a);  show?
answer: Something like [I@ and a hex code, not the numbers.

sentences.c1: Something like [I@ and a hex code, not the numbers.

items.text: Starting values go in square brackets, like int[] a = [v0, v1];.
Starting values go in braces, like int[] a = {v0, v1};.
System.out.println(a) prints the elements of the array a.
Printing an array variable prints its memory address (a hexadecimal integer like @f62373), not its elements.
An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says.
The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.
x = i++ and x = ++i store the same value in x.
Both increment i, but ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.
i++ increases i by 2.
i++ (and ++i) increases i by exactly 1.
i = i++ increases i by 1.
i++ evaluates to the old value, so i = i++ stores the old value back.
The number of brackets in an array type or initializer is the array's length.
Brackets give the number of dimensions; the length is set at creation.
++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass
The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s.
Identity: an array initializer is a brace-enclosed, comma-separated list of values that creates and fills an array in one step.

Declarative: 'T[] a = {v0, ..., vk};' declares, creates (no new needed) and initializes an array of length k+1. For 2-D arrays each row is its own brace list. The bare form is legal only in a declaration; elsewhere write new T[]{...}.
Sequencing: the array of length k+1 is created, the initializer expressions are evaluated left to right and stored in a[0], a[1], ..., a[k], and then the reference is assigned to a.
Result: int[] a = {1, 2, 3}; gives a.length == 3, a[0] == 1, a[2] == 3. String[] suit = {"Clubs", "Diamonds", "Hearts", "Spades"}; gives suit.length == 4.
State transition: one execution creates one array holding the listed values and sets the variable to its reference.
An initializer implies array creation: it is shorthand for new T[k+1] followed by k+1 element assignments, so new is not written.
Plan/role: build small fixed tables of constants known when the program is written (suits, ranks, month names), usually used as fixed-value lookup tables.

Conservation: adding or removing a value changes the length. Code that uses a.length (e.g. rank.length) adapts, while code with a hard-coded size breaks. Reordering values changes which index holds which value.
Applicability: use an initializer when all values are known at compile time and the array is small. When the values must be computed at run time, create the array with new and fill it in a loop.
rule broken: Initializer values are enclosed in braces. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: brackets are used, as in int[] a = [1, 2, 3]; (illegal start of expression)
rule broken: The bare {...} form is allowed only in a declaration. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: a = {1, 2, 3}; used as a later assignment (array constants can only be used in initializers)
rule broken: Each value must be assignable to the element type. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: int[] a = {1, 2.5}; (incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int)

question: Write a loop that multiplies every element by 10.
answer: for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) a[i] = a[i] * 10;

sentences.c1: for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) a[i] = a[i] * 10;

items.text: x = y stores the value of y in x (a statement with a side effect); x == y only tests whether the two values are equal and gives a boolean. Writing = where == is meant is a compile error with int operands and a silent bug with boolean operands.
i++ is shorthand for the assignment i = i + 1.
Writes for (int i = 0, i < n, i++).
The three parts of a for header are separated by semicolons; commas only separate several statements inside the init or the update part.
Writes int x = 5; ... int x = 10; to change x.
A declaration gives a variable its name and type; a later change of value is an assignment statement such as x = 10;, not a second declaration.
An array cannot have length 0.
new int[0] is a legal array of length 0.
x = i++ and x = ++i store the same value in x.
Both increment i, but ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.
i = i++ increases i by 1.
i++ evaluates to the old value, so i = i++ stores the old value back.
++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass
The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s.
new int[n] has slots 0 to n, inclusive.
The slots are 0 to n - 1.
i++ increases i by 2.
i++ (and ++i) increases i by exactly 1.
Integer division: / applied to two integer operands, giving the whole-number quotient with the fractional part discarded.
If both operands of / are integral types, the result is an integer that rounds toward 0 (-14 / 3 is -4). If either operand is a double, the division is floating point.

Each / is evaluated when its turn comes (precedence, then left to right), using the types of its own two operands. Promoting the result to double, by a cast or by assignment, happens only afterwards and cannot restore the lost fraction.
q = a / b stores the truncated quotient in q and leaves a and b unchanged. If b is 0, an ArithmeticException stops execution before anything is stored.
/ and % on ints are paired: q = a / b and r = a % b always satisfy a = b * q + r.
Normalizing counts must divide as doubles. With two ints, counts / total truncates to 0 whenever counts < total.
% gives the remainder of the same truncating division: (a / b) * b + a % b == a.
Quotient plans: unit conversion (76 / 12 feet), dropping a digit (n / 10), finding a midpoint ((lo + hi) / 2), and computing a bucket or row index (i / cols).

Making one operand a double (10.0 / 3) keeps the fraction (3.333...). Casting after the division does not. Multiplying before dividing preserves precision (59 * 100 / 60 is 98). Changing an operand's sign changes only the quotient's sign, since rounding is toward zero.

Use integer division when you want the whole quotient (units, digits, indices, half a size). When a fraction is needed, make one operand a double (10.0 / 3 or (double) a / b) rather than turning every variable into a double.

Identity: an array initializer is a brace-enclosed, comma-separated list of values that creates and fills an array in one step.

Declarative: 'T[] a = {v0, ..., vk};' declares, creates (no new needed) and initializes an array of length k+1. For 2-D arrays each row is its own brace list. The bare form is legal only in a declaration; elsewhere write new T[]{...}.
Sequencing: the array of length k+1 is created, the initializer expressions are evaluated left to right and stored in a[0], a[1], ..., a[k], and then the reference is assigned to a.

Plan/role: reserve storage for a number of values that may be known only at run time (e.g. N from the command line), before any value is stored.

rule broken: The dimension expression of new must be >= 0. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: the size evaluates to a negative int, e.g. a negative command-line value, or int overflow such as new int[N*N*N*N] with N = 1000 (NegativeArraySizeException)
