StdIn is a booksite library of static methods that read typed values from the standard input stream: isEmpty, readInt, readDouble, readLong, readBoolean, readChar, readString, readLine, readAll.

StdIn reads from a stream that may be empty or may contain values separated by whitespace. readInt() reads the next token, parses it as an int and returns it, and the token must have the type the method expects. Outside the book's StdIn library, standard Java reads keyboard input with java.util.Scanner (nextInt(), nextDouble(), nextLine()); a token of the wrong type stops the program with InputMismatchException.

When execution reaches a read, the program blocks until a complete token is available (at the terminal, until <return>). The read then parses the token and returns, the assignment stores the value, and the next statement runs.
readInt returns an int, readDouble a double, readString a String, readBoolean a boolean. AddInts 4 with input 144 233 377 1024 prints Sum is 1778.
One read moves the input position past one token and returns its value. Assigning that value overwrites the variable's previous value. No other variable changes.
Every StdIn call takes from the same stream position, so values are delivered once, in order.
To read an unknown number of values, each read must be guarded by !StdIn.isEmpty() as the condition of a while loop whose body reads.
With `< file` the same StdIn calls read from the file instead of the keyboard. The program text does not change.
The reads must follow the file's layout: one readInt() for n first, then pairs of readInt() for each link i j until isEmpty().
The program turns the input stream into the output stream: values read with StdIn are processed and the results are written with StdOut. The two streams are independent.
StdIn values can drive StdDraw output. PlotFilter reads x, y pairs and draws a point for each, after scaling from the first four numbers.
The method called fixes the type the next token must have: readInt needs an int literal, and readDouble accepts 5 or 5.0.
Because a read can run at any point in execution, a read inside a loop lets each typed value decide the next branch.
Token reads (readInt, readString) and line reads (readLine) share one position. A token read leaves the rest of its line for the next readLine, so it is best not to mix the two.

Command-line arguments are a fixed number of strings given once when the program starts (args[]); standard input is a stream of any length read while the program runs (StdIn.readInt()). Both arrive as text and must be parsed into numbers.
StdIn brings an unbounded amount of data into a running program. The variable that receives each read plays the Sajaniemi role of most-recent holder.

Running (executing) a program is launching it with java Name so that the Java Virtual Machine follows its instructions.

Typing java followed by a class name makes the system call the main() method defined in that class and execute its statements; java Name args... also passes the command-line arguments to main. The development cycle is the same in any environment (terminal or IDE): edit the .java file, compile it with javac, run it with java.
The JVM starts at the first statement of main and ends when it finishes the last statement; statements run one by one, in order, and control returns to the system when main finishes.
The result of a run is what the program prints to the terminal (for java HelloWorld: Hello, World), or an exception message if a run-time error occurs.
One execution step runs one statement of main, which changes the program state (a variable or the output) and passes control to the next statement.
java Name runs the Name.class that javac produced, so compiling must succeed first; the run reflects the source as of the last successful compile.
A run-time error appears only while java Name executes; the JVM stops the program and prints the exception.
A logic error is seen only by running the program and comparing its output with the intended output.
A program is tested by running it on chosen inputs and comparing what it prints with what it should print.
Each small step is run and checked before the next one is added.
Purpose: make the computer carry out the program on particular inputs; running the same compiled program with different command-line arguments gives different results.

Running again with the same arguments reproduces the same output (for programs without randomness or input); changing the arguments changes the output without recompiling; editing the source changes nothing until recompiled.
Run the program to test it on chosen inputs and to see run-time and logic errors that compiling cannot find; adding print statements and rerunning is a simple way to check what is actually executing.

items.text: Naming convention: a style rule (not a language rule) for choosing identifiers. Variables and methods use lowerCamelCase, classes UpperCamelCase, constants UPPER_CASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES, and names describe meaning.

Variable names begin with a lowercase letter and capitalize each later word (firstName). Class names begin with a capital. Constants are all uppercase with _ between words. Names should indicate what the variable means.
Conventions have no execution order: the compiler checks only that an identifier is legal and declared, never whether it follows convention.
A program's output does not depend on its names: renaming total to t everywhere gives identical results.
Following or breaking a convention changes no state; it only changes how readable the code is.
Each variable's name should describe what it holds (count, sum, maxSoFar). Single letters suit only short-lived loop indices.
Constants are written in ALL_CAPS with underscores, which sets them apart from lowerCamelCase variables and signals that they never change.
Good names make each variable's role visible (sum for a gatherer, count for a counter, max for a most-wanted holder, i for a stepper), so a reader can recognize the plan without tracing.

Renaming consistently keeps the program's meaning, because what it computes does not depend on names. A misleading name (max holding a minimum) still compiles and runs the same, but readers draw wrong conclusions.
Apply the conventions to every name you write. Short names fit only tiny scopes (loop index i, coordinates x and y). No naming convention can replace the code that actually computes the value.

rule broken: A name does not compute or guarantee a value. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Trusting a descriptive name instead of the code (e.g. assuming average holds the mean although it was never divided): wrong output that the name hides.

items.text: Identity: a two-dimensional array, an array of arrays used to represent a table or matrix with M rows and N columns.
Declarative: declare double[][] a; create with new double[M][N] (rows first, then columns); refer to row i, column j as a[i][j]. Entries start at 0 (numbers) or false (boolean).
Sequencing: new double[M][N] creates an array of M references and then M row arrays of N defaults. a[i][j] evaluates a[i] (checked against a.length = M) and then [j] (checked against a[i].length).
Result: a[i][j] has the element type; a.length is the number of rows M; a[i].length is the length of row i; a[i] is a double[] row.
State transition: a[i][j] = v changes one element of row i; a[i] = new double[K] replaces the whole row i with a new array; other rows are untouched.
The transition matrix is a 2-D double array p[i][j] with one row per page; each row holds a probability distribution.
A 2-D array uses two indices, and the first chooses the row array: a[i][j] is (a[i])[j].
Since each row is a separate array, rows may have different lengths; such arrays are ragged.
Matrix operations index a[i][j] in nested loops (two for addition, three for multiplication).
The same notation extends to any number of dimensions: a[i][j][k] for double[][][].
Row-major order visits a[i][j] with the outer loop over rows i; column-major puts the loop over j outside.
Plan/role: store tables, matrices, grids and images indexed by row and column (grades by student and test, lattice intersections, pixels).
Conservation: swapping the loop order for an element-wise operation keeps the result but changes the processing order. Swapping the indices (a[j][i]) transposes and goes out of bounds when M != N.

Applicability: use a 2-D array for data naturally indexed by two integers (rows by columns). Use a ragged array when rows differ, a 1-D array when one index suffices, and higher dimensions for 3-D models.

rule broken: Indices must be within each dimension (i < a.length, j < a[i].length). Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: row and column bounds swapped in a non-square M-by-N array, or j bounded by N on a shorter ragged row (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)

% gives the remainder after integer division: 9 % 5 is 4 because 9 = 1 * 5 + 4, and 17 % 5 is 2, not 12.
"10" - 1 or "6" * "2" works because the strings look like numbers.

an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression

local variables get a default value on their own

Definite assignment: the compile-time rule that a local variable must certainly have been assigned before any read of it.

Every access of a local variable must be preceded by an assignment on every possible path, or the program does not compile. The analysis ignores run-time values, except for constant booleans and the operators && || ?:.

The compiler walks the control flow. After a declaration with no initializer the variable is unassigned, and an assignment makes it assigned on that path. Where paths merge (after if/else) it counts as assigned only if every incoming path assigned it, and an assignment inside a while body does not count after the loop.
The result appears at compile time: the code either compiles or reports 'variable x might not have been initialized'. No default value is ever produced for a local variable.
The first assignment (initialization) moves a variable from unassigned to holding a value, and only then may it be read.
A declaration without an initializer leaves the local unassigned. Writing = value in the declaration satisfies the rule at once.

A local variable has no value until it is assigned: using it first is a compile-time error. An array element is given a default value (0, 0.0, false) when the array is created with new, so it can be read before any assignment.

The rule guarantees that no program reads a meaningless value. The matching plan is to initialize counters and accumulators before the loop that updates them (int sum = 0; then sum += i inside the loop).

Moving an initialization into one branch of an if, or into a loop body, breaks compilation of the reads that follow. Adding an else branch that also assigns, or initializing at the declaration, restores it.

Initialize at the declaration whenever a sensible first value exists (0 for counters and sums). Leave the declaration bare only when every branch that follows assigns it. The rule covers local variables only: array elements and fields get default values.

rule broken: A local variable must be definitely assigned before it is read. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: A read reachable on a path with no assignment: declared without initializer, or assigned only inside an if without else, a loop body, or a switch case: 'variable might not have been initialized'.

rule broken: A blank final variable must be assigned at most once. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Assigning a final local on two paths that can both run, or again inside a loop: 'variable might already have been assigned'.

items.text: Relational operators compare two numbers to give a boolean; logical operators combine booleans into one boolean.
&& and || evaluate their second operand only when the first has not already decided the result (false && x is false, true || x is true).
Writes =< or => instead of <= and >=.
The operators are written <= and >=.
< and > mean the same thing (or a < b means a is greater than b).
a < b is true when a is smaller than b; a > b when a is larger.
90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100.
a < b < c does not compile (a < b is a boolean); a range test is written 90 <= grade && grade <= 100.
s < t compares two Strings alphabetically.
< and > are defined only for primitive types; comparing Strings with them does not compile.
you must write == true / == false to test a boolean
if (b) already tests b, so writing == true adds nothing.
= compares two values instead of assigning
x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
A condition on several values has to be written as nested if statements, one value per if.
Several conditions combine into one boolean expression with && and ||, e.g. if (x == 0 && y == 0).
In p && q, both p and q are always evaluated.
In p && q, q is evaluated only when p is true; in p || q, q is evaluated only when p is false.
Integer division: / applied to two integer operands, giving the whole-number quotient with the fractional part discarded.
If both operands of / are integral types, the result is an integer that rounds toward 0 (-14 / 3 is -4). If either operand is a double, the division is floating point.

Each / is evaluated when its turn comes (precedence, then left to right), using the types of its own two operands. Promoting the result to double, by a cast or by assignment, happens only afterwards and cannot restore the lost fraction.
q = a / b stores the truncated quotient in q and leaves a and b unchanged. If b is 0, an ArithmeticException stops execution before anything is stored.
/ and % on ints are paired: q = a / b and r = a % b always satisfy a = b * q + r.
Normalizing counts must divide as doubles. With two ints, counts / total truncates to 0 whenever counts < total.
% gives the remainder of the same truncating division: (a / b) * b + a % b == a.
Quotient plans: unit conversion (76 / 12 feet), dropping a digit (n / 10), finding a midpoint ((lo + hi) / 2), and computing a bucket or row index (i / cols).

Making one operand a double (10.0 / 3) keeps the fraction (3.333...). Casting after the division does not. Multiplying before dividing preserves precision (59 * 100 / 60 is 98). Changing an operand's sign changes only the quotient's sign, since rounding is toward zero.

Use integer division when you want the whole quotient (units, digits, indices, half a size). When a fraction is needed, make one operand a double (10.0 / 3 or (double) a / b) rather than turning every variable into a double.

rule broken: With two int operands, / discards the fraction. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Two int operands where a fraction is intended: 9/5 in a temperature formula, count / total, 1 / n, sum / n for an average.
rule broken: int division by zero is undefined. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: A divisor that evaluates to 0: ArithmeticException: / by zero.
rule broken: Integer division rounds toward zero, not down. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Negative operands where floor was expected (-7 / 2 is -3, not -4).

Comparison (relational) operators ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= are mixed-type operators: they take two operands of a numeric type and produce a boolean.

==, !=, <, <=, >, >= are defined for each primitive numeric type and produce a boolean; they have lower precedence than arithmetic and higher than boolean operators; < and > are not defined for Strings, and == on non-primitive types compares identity.
Evaluate the left operand (including its arithmetic), then the right operand; if their types differ, promote the narrower one (int to double); then compare and produce true or false.
The result is a boolean: (2 <= 2) is true, 2 < 2 is false, (x < 3.1) is true for int x = 3; any comparison involving NaN, even NaN == NaN, is false.
A comparison changes no variable and only returns a boolean, unlike =, which changes the value of the variable on its left.
A comparison is itself an expression whose value is a boolean, so it can appear anywhere a boolean is needed, including on the right of an assignment (boolean ok = x > y;).
Comparisons are the building blocks of conditions: together with boolean logic they provide the basis for decision-making.
Comparisons bind tighter than && and ||, so they are evaluated first and logical operators combine their boolean results.
Comparisons take numbers and produce a boolean; boolean values themselves can be compared only with == and != (not <), and testing them against true is unnecessary.

x = y stores the value of y in x (a statement with a side effect); x == y only tests whether the two values are equal and gives a boolean. Writing = where == is meant is a compile error with int operands and a silent bug with boolean operands.
Used to test a numeric condition: thresholds and sign checks, range tests, divisibility (n % k == 0), loop continuation (i < N), sentinel checks, and running-extreme updates (if (x > max) max = x).

Changing < to <= (or > to >=) changes the result only at the boundary value, which in a loop guard means one more or one fewer iteration (off-by-one); mirroring the comparison (a < b to b > a) preserves the value; negating it gives the complementary operator (!(a < b) is a >= b).

items.text: The for statement is a loop that packages an initialization, a loop-continuation condition and an increment in its header around a body.

Syntax: for (<initialize>; <boolean expression>; <increment>) { <statements> }, with the three parts separated by semicolons; it is, with only a few exceptions, equivalent to <initialize>; while (<boolean expression>) { <statements> <increment>; }.
Run the initializer once; then repeatedly: test the condition (stop if false), execute the body, run the update.
A for statement has no value; the passes it makes are fixed by its header: for (int i = 1; i <= N; i++) sum += i; leaves sum = N(N+1)/2, and for (int i = 2; i <= 8; i += 2) prints 2, 4, 6, 8,.
One pass: the test reads the loop variable; the body applies its changes once; the update then changes the loop variable by its rule; the initializer changes state only once, before the first test.
The for header is exactly the three loop-control slots; the body runs after the test and before the update on each pass.
A for may be the body of another for: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer one.
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) gives i each valid index 0..N-1 exactly once in increasing order, the standard way to process every array element.
A simulation runs a fixed number of trials with an outer for loop (for (int t = 0; t < T; t++)), each trial simulated inside the body.
In a for loop, continue skips the rest of the body and transfers control directly to the increment, then the next test; this is one of the few places where the for/while equivalence fails.
A variable declared in the for header is in scope only in the header and the body, so it cannot be used after the loop.
A fencepost loop is a for loop that handles one item (the first or last) outside the loop so that separators come out n-1 times for n items.
A flag search loop is a for loop that sets a boolean flag when some pass finds the target and leaves it set afterwards; the flag must be declared before the loop.
Plan: counted loop / counter-controlled repetition - do the body a known number of times, with the loop variable as a stepper (index, term number, trial number).

Rewriting a for as the equivalent while (init before, update at the end of the body) keeps behaviour, except that continue then skips the update and the loop variable stays in scope after the loop. Changing the bound or the step changes the pass count predictably (< to <= adds one pass).

items.text: The while statement is a loop (iteration statement): it repeats a body as long as a boolean condition is true.

Syntax: while (<boolean expression>) { <statements> } (braces optional for one statement). Meaning: if the expression is false do nothing; if true, execute the body, then check the expression again, and continue as long as it is true.
1. Evaluate the condition. 2. If false, skip the body and continue after the loop. 3. If true, execute the whole body, then go back to step 1.
A while statement has no value; its result is the state and output after the passes it made: e.g. TenHellos with i = 4 and i <= 10 prints 4th to 10th Hello (7 passes) and leaves i = 11.

One pass: test the condition with the current values, then (if true) apply every body statement once in order; the variables assigned in the body change and nothing else; a false test ends the loop with the state unchanged.
The loop condition is a boolean expression evaluated before every pass; the loop stops the first time it is false, so the body must eventually make it false.
do { body } while (c); means the same as while (c) { body } except that the first test is omitted, so the body runs at least once.
break exits the loop immediately, so a while loop can end either by a false test or by a break; while (true) needs a break (or is infinite).
An animation repeats clear/draw/show/pause steps inside a loop, typically one that runs indefinitely.
A convergence test is the while condition that keeps refining an estimate until the error is within tolerance, e.g. while (Math.abs(t - c/t) > epsilon * t).
The body is the block that the while repeats; it runs only after a true test and is completed before the next test.
The while condition usually tests a loop variable that is initialized before the loop and updated in the body; if the body never changes it, the loop never ends.
To trust a while loop, state what stays true on every pass and why the condition eventually becomes false (e.g. v is always a power of 2, v increases, so the loop terminates).
Binary conversion uses while loops: one to find the largest power of 2 <= N, and one to cast out powers of 2 in decreasing order.
if and while have the same form, but if tests its condition once and runs the block at most once, while while tests again after every pass and repeats the block as long as the condition is true.

Plan: indefinite (event-controlled) repetition - repeat until something happens whose number of passes is not known in advance (until convergence, until broke or goal); the condition variable is often a stepper or most-recent holder.

The computer recognises that one variable plays two roles, e.g. input value and running total, and keeps the values apart; it knows which variable is the counter and which the sum.
A variable holds one value at a time; each role (input, counter, running total) needs its own variable and explicit update.
b = a exchanges the values of a and b.
b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.
x = y checks whether x and y are equal.
x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
a = b copies the value of a into b.
Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.
A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model).
Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.
Writes name = value; to declare a new variable.
A declaration needs a type: type name = value;
a = b adds the value of b to the value already in a (the accumulator model).
a = b replaces the old value of a with the value of b; the old value is lost.
double is a primitive data type: Java's 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point type for representing real numbers.

Values are 64-bit IEEE 754 numbers (about 15 significant digits) plus the special values Infinity and NaN; +, -, *, / (and %) are defined; if at least one operand of a binary arithmetic operator is double, the operation is a floating-point operation.

Operators are applied in precedence order, left operand first; at each operator, if one operand is double the other is widened to double before the operation, and the result is rounded to the nearest double before the next operator uses it.
The result has type double: 5.0/3.0 is 1.6666666666666667, 10/3.0 is 3.3333333333333335, 1.0/0.0 is Infinity, Math.sqrt(-1.0) is NaN; println always shows a decimal part (3.0, not 3).

An assignment to a double variable stores the nearest representable value (x = x + 0.1 replaces x with the rounded sum); no double operation throws an exception, so the variable may end up holding Infinity or NaN.

Type flow decides the division: with two int operands a / b discards the fraction (10/3 is 3, and double d = 10/3; stores 3.0); if either operand is double the other is promoted and the fraction is kept (10/3.0 is 3.3333333333333335).
double and boolean never convert into each other (no cast is allowed either way); they meet only through comparisons, which take doubles and produce a boolean, e.g. (x < 3.1).
char is an integral numeric type, so a char widens automatically to double in arithmetic ('a' + 0.5 is 97.5), but a double needs an explicit cast to become a char.
Every double operation rounds its result to the nearest representable value, so double results carry rounding error that can accumulate; this is why == on computed doubles is unreliable.

double is one of the eight primitive types and the default type of decimal literals (float would need an f suffix and is not used in the book).
Used for measured or computed real quantities (physics formulas, roots, averages, probabilities); a double variable often plays the gatherer role, as in Harmonic's sum += 1.0/i.

Selection statement: `switch (expr) { case v1: ...; break; ... default: ... }` chooses among many alternatives by the value of one expression.

The selector is an int-like (char, byte, short, int), String or enum expression. Case labels are distinct constants of that type, and default is optional. Control jumps to the matching label (or to default, or past the switch), and the case statements usually end with break. Without a break, execution falls through into the statements of the next case; default runs when no case matches.

Order: evaluate the selector once; compare it with the case constants; jump to the matching label (else default, else skip the switch). Then execute the statements from there in order, through later labels, until a break or the closing brace.
A switch statement has no value. Its result is the effect of the case(s) run: with `day = 3`, the S&W day switch prints Wed. Without breaks, day = 5 would print Fri, then Sat.
One execution evaluates the selector once (any side effect in it happens once) and runs the statements of one entry point and any cases it falls into. It changes only what those statements change.
A switch replaces an if-else chain only when every test is `expr == constant` on the same expression. Range tests such as the income-bracket chain (`income < 47450`) must stay an if-else chain.
Each case is normally ended by break, which exits the switch body. Leaving it out makes that case fall into the next. Inside a loop, that break exits the switch, not the loop.

Plan: multiway dispatch or lookup. It maps one discrete value (day number, menu choice, character) to one of several actions or results. Grouped labels (`case "apple": case "banana":`) map several values to one action.

When every case ends with break, reordering the cases does not change behaviour (labels are distinct constants). Removing one break changes behaviour for that value only. Adding a default changes only values with no matching label.

Use switch for more than two mutually exclusive alternatives decided by equality of one int, char, String or enum value. Use an if-else chain for ranges, doubles or unrelated conditions. Use an array lookup (S&W 1.4) when each case only selects a value.

Nested loops are a loop inside the body of another loop: the outer loop and the inner loop.
Because loops are statements, one can be the body of another; the inner loop iterates all the way through for each iteration of the outer loop.

Outer init; outer test; [inner init; inner test; inner body; inner update; ... until the inner test fails]; rest of the outer body; outer update; outer test; ... The inner init runs again on every outer pass.
The inner body runs (outer passes) x (inner passes) times: two loops of 1..10 call printf 100 times; DivisorPattern 3 prints 3 rows of 3 entries, each row ending with its row number.
One outer pass resets the inner variable, runs the complete inner loop, executes the rest of the outer body once, and then updates the outer variable once.
Usually both loops are for loops: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer for.
Matrix addition uses two nested loops over i and j; matrix multiplication adds a third, innermost loop over k for each dot product.
A plain break ends only the innermost loop; a labeled break is needed when the inner loop must end the outer one too.
Which loop is outside decides the visiting order: row index outside gives row-major order, column index outside gives column-major order.
Plan: process every pair (i, j) - two-dimensional tables, every row x column of a matrix, every pair of elements; the outer variable is a slow stepper, the inner a fast stepper.

Swapping the outer and inner loops visits the same pairs in a different order (rows vs columns), which preserves a sum but changes printed layout; moving a statement between the inner body and the outer body changes its count from (outer x inner) to outer.

Use nested loops when the work ranges over all combinations of two indices (tables, matrices, pairs); expect running time proportional to the product of the pass counts, and prefer a single loop when the second index is a function of the first.

rule broken: Without braces, the body of an if, while or for is exactly one statement; indentation does not add statements to it. Kind: silent logic error. rule broken: The inner loop needs its own loop variable. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Redeclaring the outer variable in the inner header (for (int i ...) { for (int i ...) }): 'variable i is already defined'.

rule broken: The inner loop must update its own variable. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Writing for (int j = 0; j < N; i++) in the inner loop: j never changes, so the inner loop is infinite (or i runs out of range).

10 / 3 evaluates to 3.333....
Dividing two ints gives an int: the fractional part is discarded.
Integer division: / applied to two integer operands, giving the whole-number quotient with the fractional part discarded.
If both operands of / are integral types, the result is an integer that rounds toward 0 (-14 / 3 is -4). If either operand is a double, the division is floating point.

Each / is evaluated when its turn comes (precedence, then left to right), using the types of its own two operands. Promoting the result to double, by a cast or by assignment, happens only afterwards and cannot restore the lost fraction.
q = a / b stores the truncated quotient in q and leaves a and b unchanged. If b is 0, an ArithmeticException stops execution before anything is stored.
/ and % on ints are paired: q = a / b and r = a % b always satisfy a = b * q + r.
Normalizing counts must divide as doubles. With two ints, counts / total truncates to 0 whenever counts < total.
% gives the remainder of the same truncating division: (a / b) * b + a % b == a.
Quotient plans: unit conversion (76 / 12 feet), dropping a digit (n / 10), finding a midpoint ((lo + hi) / 2), and computing a bucket or row index (i / cols).

Making one operand a double (10.0 / 3) keeps the fraction (3.333...). Casting after the division does not. Multiplying before dividing preserves precision (59 * 100 / 60 is 98). Changing an operand's sign changes only the quotient's sign, since rounding is toward zero.

Use integer division when you want the whole quotient (units, digits, indices, half a size). When a fraction is needed, make one operand a double (10.0 / 3 or (double) a / b) rather than turning every variable into a double.

rule broken: With two int operands, / discards the fraction. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Two int operands where a fraction is intended: 9/5 in a temperature formula, count / total, 1 / n, sum / n for an average.
rule broken: int division by zero is undefined. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: A divisor that evaluates to 0: ArithmeticException: / by zero.
rule broken: Integer division rounds toward zero, not down. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Negative operands where floor was expected (-7 / 2 is -3, not -4).

question: Explain in plain English what these three lines do.

items.text: a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values.
A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.
b = a exchanges the values of a and b.
b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.
Variable swap: the three-assignment idiom that exchanges the values of two variables through a temporary variable.
int t = a; a = b; b = t; exchanges a and b. The temporary t must have their type, and the three statements must run in exactly this order.
Step 1 saves a in t. Step 2 overwrites a with b. Step 3 copies the saved value from t into b. Each step reads values left by the previous one.
Starting from a = 1234 and b = 99, the swap ends with a = 99, b = 1234 and t = 1234.
Each of the three statements changes exactly one variable: first t, then a, then b.
A swap is three assignments whose order matters, because each one overwrites the old value of its left variable.
Plan: exchange. It is used to reorder two values (make a <= b), and inside sorting and shuffling of arrays. t plays Sajaniemi's temporary role.

Reordering the steps (int t = a; b = t; a = b;) breaks the swap: both variables end up holding a's value. Dropping the temporary breaks it the same way. Running the correct swap twice restores the originals, so a swap is its own inverse.

Use the swap when two variables or array elements must exchange values (sorting, shuffling, ordering a pair). It is not needed when you only need a new variable holding the larger value, or when you can compute directly into new variables.

rule broken: An assignment overwrites its target, so a value about to be overwritten must be saved first. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Swapping without a temporary (a = b; b = a;) or in the wrong order: both variables end with the same value whenever a != b.
rule broken: The temporary must have the type of the values being swapped. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Using int t to swap doubles: 'possible lossy conversion from double to int'.

items.text: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--).
The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...).
A return inside a loop does not end the loop; it sets a value each pass (the last one is returned) or returns several values.
When return executes, the method ends at once, so the loop stops on that pass.
for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times.
Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect.
Omits braces around a single-statement body of if, for or while.
Braces are optional for a single-statement body, but using them anyway avoids bugs when statements are added later.
x[i] -= y sets x[i] to -y (reads -= as assignment of a negated value).
x[i] -= y means x[i] = x[i] - y: it subtracts y from the current value.
The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value.
The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value.
A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats.
Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.
if (x > 0); System.out.println("positive"); prints only for positive x.
The ; ends the if with an empty statement, so the next line always runs.
A compound assignment operator (+=, -=, *=, /=, %=) is an assignment shorthand that combines a binary operation with storing the result back in the left-hand variable.

x op= e is equivalent to x = (T) ((x) op (e)) where T is the type of x, with x evaluated only once; it works for any arithmetic operator in any primitive numeric type. x op= e means x = (T)(x op e), with a hidden cast to the type T of x: with int x = 3, x += 0.5 compiles and leaves 3, while x = x + 0.5 does not compile.
Evaluate x and save its value, then evaluate e, then compute x op e, cast to x's type, and store into x.

The new value of x is (T)(old x op e) and is also the expression's value: each starting from int x = 7: x += 3 gives 10, x /= 2 gives 3, and x += 0.5 gives 7 (7.5 truncated) instead of a compile error.
One execution changes exactly one variable, x, from its old value (sum += x[i] turns sum = 1 into 1 + 4 = 5).
x op= e is shorthand for the assignment x = x op e, so the new value depends on the old one (x is read, then written).
x op= e includes a hidden narrowing cast to the type of x: with int x = 1, x += 1.7 compiles (as x = (int)(x + 1.7), giving 2) while x = x + 1.7 does not.
i++, ++i and i += 1 all add 1 to i; ++ and -- change a variable only by one and are normally used for integers, while i += k works for any amount and with any arithmetic operator (-=, *=, /=, %=).
Plan/role: the update step of a gatherer (sum += a[i], product *= i) or of a stepper with a step other than 1 (i += 2).

For a variable of the same type as the result, replacing x op= e by x = x op e preserves behaviour; when x is narrower (int x, double e), x = x op e no longer compiles, so the two are not always interchangeable. Swapping += and -= reverses the effect of each pass.

Use op= for in-place updates of accumulators, products and counters with steps other than 1; avoid it when x is int and e is fractional (silent truncation), and use explicit x = x op e when the cast should be visible.

rule broken: x op= e silently casts the result to the type of x. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: int total = 0; total += 0.5 * k; or int avg = 7; avg /= 2.0;: fractional parts are discarded (avg becomes 3) without a compiler error.
rule broken: =- is assignment of a negated value, not -=. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Typing x =- y for x -= y: compiles as x = -y.

if and while have the same form, but if tests its condition once and runs the block at most once, while while tests again after every pass and repeats the block as long as the condition is true.

+ adds when both operands are numbers and concatenates when either operand is a String, converting the other operand to a String. It is left-associative, so 1 + 2 + "3" is "33" but "1" + 2 + 3 is "123".
&& and || evaluate their second operand only when the first has not already decided the result (false && x is false, true || x is true).
9 % 5 means 9 minus 5 (a % b subtracts b from a).
% gives the remainder after integer division: 9 % 5 is 4 because 9 = 1 * 5 + 4, and 17 % 5 is 2, not 12.
a % b is never negative, and integer division of a negative number rounds down.
a / b rounds toward 0 and a % b takes the sign of a: -14 / 3 is -4 and -14 % 3 is -2.
An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true.
An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it.
17 % 5 is 3 (the quotient).
% returns the remainder, so 17 % 5 is 2.
For and while loops end when the condition becomes true.
A for or while loop ends when its condition becomes false.
If a loop condition is false at first but would become true later, the loop still runs (it repeats or skips until the condition is true, then runs until it is false).
A while loop whose condition is false at the first test runs zero times; nothing later revives it.
How many times a loop runs is decided by what the program is meant to do, so it may go on after its condition is false.
The loop runs only while its condition is true when tested; it stops at the first false test.
& and | are the same as && and || for conditions, so either can be used.
&& and || skip the right operand when the left decides the result; & and | always evaluate both, which fails when the right side depends on the left (e.g. x != 0 & y / x > 1).
System.out.print(x) is a library method call (on the PrintStream System.out) that displays x in the terminal without ending the line.
print(String s) prints the string (or "null" for a null reference); print(int) etc. print the value's string form; no line terminator is written.
The argument expression is evaluated first, converted to a string, then its characters are written at the current output position; the next output continues right after them.

Output is exactly the characters of the value (a string literal without its quotes, a number in decimal) and nothing else: print("Goodbye, "); println("cruel world"); prints Goodbye, cruel world on one line.
One call appends the value's characters to the output and leaves the cursor on the same line; it changes no variable and returns nothing (void).
System.out.print(s); is a statement, so its output appears at its place in the statement sequence.
print("s") outputs exactly the characters between the quotes, without the quotes; spaces inside the quotes are printed.
print leaves the cursor on the same line; println ends the line; a line built from several prints should end with println.
Purpose: build one line of output from several pieces (a prompt, labels and values) before ending it with println.
Changing print to println (or back) moves the following output to a new line (or the same line) but keeps the characters printed; swapping two print statements swaps their text.

rule broken: Finish a line of print calls with println. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: the last output of the program is a print: on some systems the text is held and not shown, or the prompt appears on the same line
Use print when more output must follow on the same line (prompts, items in a row); use println to end a line, and printf when the number format matters.
rule broken: A method call needs parentheses and correct case. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: System.out.print "x"; or System.out.Print(x)

items.text: a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values.
A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.
y = x + k; makes y always equal to x + k, so when x changes later, y changes too.
y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
a^2 computes a squared.
Java has no exponent operator; ^ is exclusive or, and a * a or Math.pow(a, 2) computes a squared.
Writes a + b = c; or 7 = a; as if = were a math equation.
The left side of an assignment must be a single variable; only the right side can be an expression.
Writes int x = 5; ... int x = 10; to change x.
A declaration gives a variable its name and type; a later change of value is an assignment statement such as x = 10;, not a second declaration.
b = a exchanges the values of a and b.
b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.
x = y checks whether x and y are equal.
x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
a = b copies the value of a into b.
Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.
Identity: an array access expression; a[i] names the single element variable at position i of the array a refers to.
Declarative: the index is any int-valued expression in square brackets; the valid indices of an array of length n are 0 to n-1, and an access outside that range throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Sequencing: the array reference is evaluated before the index; the index expression is fully evaluated with current variable values; the bounds are checked; then the element is fetched or, on the left of =, becomes the target. In a[i] = a[j], the target a[i] is located before a[j] is read.
Result: a[i] has the element type and the value currently stored at position i. For int[] a = {5, 7, 9}, a[1] is 7 and a[0] + a[2] is 14.
State transition: reading a[i] changes nothing. a[i] = v changes only element i (i, a and all other elements are unchanged), and a[i]++ adds 1 to that one element.
An element can be indexed only after the array is created, and the n given to new sets the valid indices 0..n-1.
A traversal uses the loop variable as the index, so the same expression a[i] reaches a different element on each pass.
Every index value is checked against 0 and a.length at run time; any other value throws.
a[i] on a 2-D array yields row i (itself a 1-D array), and a[i][j] then indexes into that row.
The exchange reads and writes elements only through their indices: t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t.
A lookup table uses a data value as the index (months[m]), so the data must lie in 0..length-1.
Indices start at 0, so the last element is a[N-1]; misreading this convention is the usual source of off-by-one errors.
Plan/role: random access, reaching any element directly by its position in constant time (address plus index), so code touches only the elements it needs.

Conservation: changing the index expression (i to i+1 or i-1) shifts which element is touched and can leave the bounds at the ends. Writing a[a[i]] instead of a[i] uses an element value as the index, a different access entirely. Changing what is stored never changes the positions.

Applicability: index when you need a particular element by position, or when the position is computed from data (counts[score]++, months[m]). When every value is processed in order and the position is never needed, an enhanced for loop is simpler.

rule broken: The index must be in 0..a.length-1. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: index < 0 or >= a.length, e.g. a[a.length], a[i+1] on the last pass, a[i-1] at i = 0, a[0] of an empty array (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)

System.out.println("x is 5"); sets x to 5 (text inside the quotes is run as code).

Code common to both branches belongs before or after the if-else.
The else branch of an if-else statement always executes.

The if-else statement is a two-way conditional: it executes one of two statements (or blocks) depending on a boolean condition.
Syntax: if (<boolean expression>) <statements T> else <statements F>; it executes one or the other, but not both: T if the condition is true, F otherwise.
Evaluate the condition once; if true execute the then branch, otherwise execute the else branch; then continue with the statement after the whole if-else (the condition is not re-tested).
Exactly one branch's effects occur; e.g. if (x > y) max = x; else max = y; leaves max equal to the larger value, and the coin flip prints either Heads or Tails, never both.
One execution reads the condition's variables and applies the effects of exactly one branch; a change made by the then branch to the condition's variables cannot cause the else branch to run.
if-else is an if with a second branch for the false case; dropping the else gives a plain if in which the false case does nothing.
Either branch may itself be an if or if-else, which nests conditionals; without braces an inner else pairs with the innermost if.
c ? a : b is the expression form of if (c) v = a; else v = b;: it yields a value of one branch, evaluating only the selected operand.
An else-if chain is an if-else whose else part is another if-else, repeated; the final else catches all remaining cases.
Plan: two-way choice / alternative action - compute one of two results (max of two values, heads or tails, error message or quotient).

Swapping the two branches and negating the condition preserves behaviour; swapping the branches alone inverts it. Replacing if-else with two separate ifs is not equivalent when the then branch changes a variable used in the condition.

rule broken: else takes no condition: it is the branch for the false case of the preceding if; a further test needs else if (...). Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Writing else (x > 0) stmt; the compiler reads (x > 0) as the start of an expression statement, which is not a valid statement, and reports an error.

rule broken: Code common to both branches belongs before or after the if-else. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A statement duplicated in both branches and later edited in only one: the two cases silently diverge.
rule broken: An else must directly follow the then statement of an if. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: if (c) x = 1; y = 2; else x = 0;: the else has no matching if ('else without if').

items.text: 9 % 5 means 9 minus 5 (a % b subtracts b from a).
% gives the remainder after integer division: 9 % 5 is 4 because 9 = 1 * 5 + 4, and 17 % 5 is 2, not 12.
a % b is never negative, and integer division of a negative number rounds down.
a / b rounds toward 0 and a % b takes the sign of a: -14 / 3 is -4 and -14 % 3 is -2.
17 % 5 is 3 (the quotient).
% returns the remainder, so 17 % 5 is 2.
"10" - 1 or "6" * "2" works because the strings look like numbers.
Arithmetic operators other than + are not defined for Strings; a String of digits must first be converted to a number, e.g. with Integer.parseInt.
a^2 computes a squared.
Java has no exponent operator; ^ is exclusive or, and a * a or Math.pow(a, 2) computes a squared.
Remainder operator %: the binary operator that gives the remainder after dividing a by b.
For ints, a % b is defined so that (a / b) * b + a % b equals a. The result takes the sign of a, % by zero throws ArithmeticException, and % also works on doubles.
Evaluate a, then b, take the quotient rounded toward 0, and give what is left over. % has the same precedence as * and /, and they group left to right.
r = a % b stores a remainder smaller in size than b and leaves a and b unchanged. If b is 0, ArithmeticException is thrown before anything is stored.
% is the companion of integer division, since a == (a / b) * b + a % b. Both use the same quotient rounded toward 0.
Plans: divisibility and parity tests (x % 2 == 0), digit extraction (x % 10), cyclic wrap-around ((i + 1) % n), leap-year rules, and splitting units (76 % 12 inches).

Negating a flips the remainder's sign, so n % 2 == 1 fails for negative odd n while n % 2 != 0 still works. Changing the divisor changes the cycle length. Swapping % with / swaps the remainder for the quotient.

Use % for divisibility, parity, digits, cyclic indices and unit splitting. Do not use it for percentages (use * / 100.0), and do not use it where a non-negative mathematical mod is needed for negative values (adjust the result or use Math.floorMod).

rule broken: % is the remainder, not a percentage. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Writing price % 15 for 15 percent of price.

items.text: A condition on several values has to be written as nested if statements, one value per if.

& only works on bits, so p & q cannot be used with booleans.
Java also has a & operator, which the book does not use; logical and is written &&.
a || b && c is evaluated left to right as (a || b) && c.
&& binds tighter than ||, so it is a || (b && c).
& and | are the same as && and || for conditions, so either can be used.
&& and || skip the right operand when the left decides the result; & and | always evaluate both, which fails when the right side depends on the left (e.g. x != 0 & y / x > 1).
Logical (boolean) operators: && (and), || (or) and ! (not), which take boolean operands and produce a boolean.
a && b is true if both operands are true and false otherwise; a || b is false if both are false and true otherwise; !a is the opposite of a; these definitions are given in full by truth tables.
! is applied before && and ||, and && before ||; the left operand is evaluated first, and for && and || the right operand is evaluated only when the left has not already decided the result.
The result is a boolean: with x = 10, x > 0 && x < 10 is false and x < 0 || x > 10 is false; true || anything is true.
The operators themselves change no variable; any side effect inside the right operand (i++, a method call) happens only if that operand is evaluated.
Combining boolean sub-expressions with &&, || and ! yields another boolean expression, so arbitrarily complex conditions can be built with parentheses.
&& and || are the short-circuit operators: in a guard such as (x != 0 && y / x > 1) the operand order matters, because the right test runs only when the left one allows it.
Comparisons bind tighter than && and ||, so comparisons are evaluated first and their boolean results are then combined (month >= 1 && month <= 12).
^ on booleans is a further logical operator, true exactly when the operands differ (it equals (a || b) && !(a && b)), but unlike && and || it always evaluates both operands.
De Morgan's laws rewrite negated && / || expressions: !(A && B) is !A || !B and !(A || B) is !A && !B.
The operands must be boolean, and the result is boolean; int operands are a compile-time error.

Used to combine several conditions into one test: a range check (lo <= x && x <= hi), alternatives (x == 0 || y == 0), a guard followed by the real test (i < n && a[i] != 0), or a rule built step by step as in LeapYear.

Swapping && for || changes the meaning; negating a whole condition requires De Morgan (negate each term and flip the operator); swapping the operands of && or || keeps the truth value but can change which side effects or exceptions occur.

Use && and || to combine conditions into a single test, ordering operands so that cheap or protective tests come first; use nested ifs only when the cases need different actions; do not use & and | for conditions.

rule broken: Conditions are combined with && and ||; & and | evaluate both operands. Kind: run-time exception. rule broken: && has higher precedence than ||. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Mixed && and || without parentheses intended to group the || first, e.g. a || b && c meant as (a || b) && c.

`do { <statements> } while (<boolean expression>);` (note the final semicolon) means the same as the corresponding while loop except that the first test of the condition is omitted. (Spec: JLS §14.13.)
Order: execute the body; evaluate the condition; if true, execute the body again and re-test; stop the first time the condition is false at the bottom test.
do-while produces no value. Its result is the state after the last pass. In the unit-disk example, x and y end inside the disk after about 4/π ≈ 1.27 passes on average.

One pass runs every statement of the body once (e.g. new random x and y) and then evaluates the condition, a boolean that decides whether another pass follows. The test changes nothing unless it has side effects.
do { S } while (c); equals `S; while (c) { S }`. If c is initially true it behaves exactly like `while (c) { S }`; if c is initially false it still runs S once where the while runs it zero times.

rule broken: The body runs at least once even if the condition is false. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Using do-while for a task that must allow zero passes (e.g. processing an empty input or N = 0): one spurious pass runs.

items.text: The for statement is a loop that packages an initialization, a loop-continuation condition and an increment in its header around a body.

Syntax: for (<initialize>; <boolean expression>; <increment>) { <statements> }, with the three parts separated by semicolons; it is, with only a few exceptions, equivalent to <initialize>; while (<boolean expression>) { <statements> <increment>; }.
Run the initializer once; then repeatedly: test the condition (stop if false), execute the body, run the update.
A for statement has no value; the passes it makes are fixed by its header: for (int i = 1; i <= N; i++) sum += i; leaves sum = N(N+1)/2, and for (int i = 2; i <= 8; i += 2) prints 2, 4, 6, 8,.
One pass: the test reads the loop variable; the body applies its changes once; the update then changes the loop variable by its rule; the initializer changes state only once, before the first test.
The for header is exactly the three loop-control slots; the body runs after the test and before the update on each pass.
A for may be the body of another for: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer one.
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) gives i each valid index 0..N-1 exactly once in increasing order, the standard way to process every array element.
A simulation runs a fixed number of trials with an outer for loop (for (int t = 0; t < T; t++)), each trial simulated inside the body.
In a for loop, continue skips the rest of the body and transfers control directly to the increment, then the next test; this is one of the few places where the for/while equivalence fails.
A variable declared in the for header is in scope only in the header and the body, so it cannot be used after the loop.
A fencepost loop is a for loop that handles one item (the first or last) outside the loop so that separators come out n-1 times for n items.
A flag search loop is a for loop that sets a boolean flag when some pass finds the target and leaves it set afterwards; the flag must be declared before the loop.
Plan: counted loop / counter-controlled repetition - do the body a known number of times, with the loop variable as a stepper (index, term number, trial number).

Rewriting a for as the equivalent while (init before, update at the end of the body) keeps behaviour, except that continue then skips the update and the loop variable stays in scope after the loop. Changing the bound or the step changes the pass count predictably (< to <= adds one pass).

Declarative: the index is any int-valued expression in square brackets; the valid indices of an array of length n are 0 to n-1, and an access outside that range throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Sequencing: the array reference is evaluated before the index; the index expression is fully evaluated with current variable values; the bounds are checked; then the element is fetched or, on the left of =, becomes the target. In a[i] = a[j], the target a[i] is located before a[j] is read.
Result: a[i] has the element type and the value currently stored at position i. For int[] a = {5, 7, 9}, a[1] is 7 and a[0] + a[2] is 14.
State transition: reading a[i] changes nothing. a[i] = v changes only element i (i, a and all other elements are unchanged), and a[i]++ adds 1 to that one element.
An element can be indexed only after the array is created, and the n given to new sets the valid indices 0..n-1.
A traversal uses the loop variable as the index, so the same expression a[i] reaches a different element on each pass.
Every index value is checked against 0 and a.length at run time; any other value throws.
a[i] on a 2-D array yields row i (itself a 1-D array), and a[i][j] then indexes into that row.
The exchange reads and writes elements only through their indices: t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t.
A lookup table uses a data value as the index (months[m]), so the data must lie in 0..length-1.
Indices start at 0, so the last element is a[N-1]; misreading this convention is the usual source of off-by-one errors.
Plan/role: random access, reaching any element directly by its position in constant time (address plus index), so code touches only the elements it needs.

items.text: The for statement is a loop that packages an initialization, a loop-continuation condition and an increment in its header around a body.

Syntax: for (<initialize>; <boolean expression>; <increment>) { <statements> }, with the three parts separated by semicolons; it is, with only a few exceptions, equivalent to <initialize>; while (<boolean expression>) { <statements> <increment>; }.
Run the initializer once; then repeatedly: test the condition (stop if false), execute the body, run the update.
A for statement has no value; the passes it makes are fixed by its header: for (int i = 1; i <= N; i++) sum += i; leaves sum = N(N+1)/2, and for (int i = 2; i <= 8; i += 2) prints 2, 4, 6, 8,.
One pass: the test reads the loop variable; the body applies its changes once; the update then changes the loop variable by its rule; the initializer changes state only once, before the first test.
The for header is exactly the three loop-control slots; the body runs after the test and before the update on each pass.
A for may be the body of another for: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer one.
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) gives i each valid index 0..N-1 exactly once in increasing order, the standard way to process every array element.
A simulation runs a fixed number of trials with an outer for loop (for (int t = 0; t < T; t++)), each trial simulated inside the body.
In a for loop, continue skips the rest of the body and transfers control directly to the increment, then the next test; this is one of the few places where the for/while equivalence fails.
A variable declared in the for header is in scope only in the header and the body, so it cannot be used after the loop.
A fencepost loop is a for loop that handles one item (the first or last) outside the loop so that separators come out n-1 times for n items.
A flag search loop is a for loop that sets a boolean flag when some pass finds the target and leaves it set afterwards; the flag must be declared before the loop.
Plan: counted loop / counter-controlled repetition - do the body a known number of times, with the loop variable as a stepper (index, term number, trial number).

Rewriting a for as the equivalent while (init before, update at the end of the body) keeps behaviour, except that continue then skips the update and the loop variable stays in scope after the loop. Changing the bound or the step changes the pass count predictably (< to <= adds one pass).

rule broken: The three parts of a for header are separated by semicolons; commas only separate several statements inside the init or the update. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Writing for (int i = 0, i < n, i++): the compiler parses the commas as more declarators in the init and reports a syntax error.

items.text: StdIn is a booksite library of static methods that read typed values from the standard input stream: isEmpty, readInt, readDouble, readLong, readBoolean, readChar, readString, readLine, readAll.

StdIn reads from a stream that may be empty or may contain values separated by whitespace. readInt() reads the next token, parses it as an int and returns it, and the token must have the type the method expects. Outside the book's StdIn library, standard Java reads keyboard input with java.util.Scanner (nextInt(), nextDouble(), nextLine()); a token of the wrong type stops the program with InputMismatchException.

When execution reaches a read, the program blocks until a complete token is available (at the terminal, until <return>). The read then parses the token and returns, the assignment stores the value, and the next statement runs.
readInt returns an int, readDouble a double, readString a String, readBoolean a boolean. AddInts 4 with input 144 233 377 1024 prints Sum is 1778.
One read moves the input position past one token and returns its value. Assigning that value overwrites the variable's previous value. No other variable changes.
Every StdIn call takes from the same stream position, so values are delivered once, in order.
To read an unknown number of values, each read must be guarded by !StdIn.isEmpty() as the condition of a while loop whose body reads.
With `< file` the same StdIn calls read from the file instead of the keyboard. The program text does not change.
The reads must follow the file's layout: one readInt() for n first, then pairs of readInt() for each link i j until isEmpty().
The program turns the input stream into the output stream: values read with StdIn are processed and the results are written with StdOut. The two streams are independent.
StdIn values can drive StdDraw output. PlotFilter reads x, y pairs and draws a point for each, after scaling from the first four numbers.
The method called fixes the type the next token must have: readInt needs an int literal, and readDouble accepts 5 or 5.0.
Because a read can run at any point in execution, a read inside a loop lets each typed value decide the next branch.
Token reads (readInt, readString) and line reads (readLine) share one position. A token read leaves the rest of its line for the next readLine, so it is best not to mix the two.

Command-line arguments are a fixed number of strings given once when the program starts (args[]); standard input is a stream of any length read while the program runs (StdIn.readInt()). Both arrive as text and must be parsed into numbers.
StdIn brings an unbounded amount of data into a running program. The variable that receives each read plays the Sajaniemi role of most-recent holder.

items.text: For ints a and b, / gives the whole quotient q and % gives the remainder r, so that a = b * q + r.
args[k] is always a String, so Integer.parseInt(args[k]) is needed before it can be used as a number.
How many times a loop runs is decided by what the program is meant to do, so it may go on after its condition is false.
The loop runs only while its condition is true when tested; it stops at the first false test.

Counting starts at 0: the first argument is args[0], the second args[1].
a^2 computes a squared.
Java has no exponent operator; ^ is exclusive or, and a * a or Math.pow(a, 2) computes a squared.
The first element of a is a[1].
Numbering begins with 0; the first element is a[0].
"10" - 1 or "6" * "2" works because the strings look like numbers.
Arithmetic operators other than + are not defined for Strings; a String of digits must first be converted to a number, e.g. with Integer.parseInt.
new int[n] has slots 0 to n, inclusive.
The slots are 0 to n - 1.
After i changes, X[i] still refers to the element at the old value of i.
a[i] is evaluated with the current value of i each time it is used.
9 % 5 means 9 minus 5 (a % b subtracts b from a).
% gives the remainder after integer division: 9 % 5 is 4 because 9 = 1 * 5 + 4, and 17 % 5 is 2, not 12.
Integer division: / applied to two integer operands, giving the whole-number quotient with the fractional part discarded.
If both operands of / are integral types, the result is an integer that rounds toward 0 (-14 / 3 is -4). If either operand is a double, the division is floating point.

Each / is evaluated when its turn comes (precedence, then left to right), using the types of its own two operands. Promoting the result to double, by a cast or by assignment, happens only afterwards and cannot restore the lost fraction.
q = a / b stores the truncated quotient in q and leaves a and b unchanged. If b is 0, an ArithmeticException stops execution before anything is stored.
/ and % on ints are paired: q = a / b and r = a % b always satisfy a = b * q + r.
Normalizing counts must divide as doubles. With two ints, counts / total truncates to 0 whenever counts < total.
% gives the remainder of the same truncating division: (a / b) * b + a % b == a.
Quotient plans: unit conversion (76 / 12 feet), dropping a digit (n / 10), finding a midpoint ((lo + hi) / 2), and computing a bucket or row index (i / cols).

Making one operand a double (10.0 / 3) keeps the fraction (3.333...). Casting after the division does not. Multiplying before dividing preserves precision (59 * 100 / 60 is 98). Changing an operand's sign changes only the quotient's sign, since rounding is toward zero.

Use integer division when you want the whole quotient (units, digits, indices, half a size). When a fraction is needed, make one operand a double (10.0 / 3 or (double) a / b) rather than turning every variable into a double.

rule broken: With two int operands, / discards the fraction. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Two int operands where a fraction is intended: 9/5 in a temperature formula, count / total, 1 / n, sum / n for an average.
rule broken: int division by zero is undefined. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: A divisor that evaluates to 0: ArithmeticException: / by zero.
rule broken: Integer division rounds toward zero, not down. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Negative operands where floor was expected (-7 / 2 is -3, not -4).

A sequence of digits is an int literal only if its value falls within the int range; for larger values the book advises the long type.
A trace is a table of the values of the program's variables after each statement, used to examine what code does.

A trace has one column per variable and one row per executed statement, in execution order; each row shows the value of every variable after that statement, with a declared but unassigned variable shown as undefined.

Follow the flow of control: take the next statement to execute (re-visiting loop bodies on each pass), evaluate it using the current row's values, and write a new row with the variables it changed; continue until the program ends.
The last row gives the final values (and any printed output follows from them): for int t = a; a = b; b = t; starting from a = 1234, b = 99, the final row is a = 99, b = 1234, t = 1234.
Each row differs from the previous one only in the variable(s) assigned by that statement; all other columns are copied unchanged.
Each assignment statement produces the next row of the trace, changing exactly the column of the variable on its left-hand side.
A test needs an expected result, and the expected result comes from tracing what the program should do, step by step.
Used to check or discover what a piece of code does (e.g. convince yourself that three statements swap a and b) and to debug; tracing a few rows often reveals the purpose of the whole.

A trace shows the effect of a change: reordering the swap's statements (int t = a; b = t; a = b;) produces a different final row in which both variables hold the original a; the trace of the correct swap keeps the invariant that the old value of a is saved in t before a is overwritten.

Trace small or unfamiliar code, loops and suspected bugs by hand; for larger programs, reason about what the parts compute (roles, invariants) or let the program print its variables, since a mental trace can hold only a few values at once.

rule broken: Each row must be computed from the current values, in execution order. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Long traces or loops that overload working memory: stale or wrong values carried into later rows, giving a wrong predicted output.

Comparison (relational) operators ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= are mixed-type operators: they take two operands of a numeric type and produce a boolean.

==, !=, <, <=, >, >= are defined for each primitive numeric type and produce a boolean; they have lower precedence than arithmetic and higher than boolean operators; < and > are not defined for Strings, and == on non-primitive types compares identity.
Evaluate the left operand (including its arithmetic), then the right operand; if their types differ, promote the narrower one (int to double); then compare and produce true or false.
The result is a boolean: (2 <= 2) is true, 2 < 2 is false, (x < 3.1) is true for int x = 3; any comparison involving NaN, even NaN == NaN, is false.
A comparison changes no variable and only returns a boolean, unlike =, which changes the value of the variable on its left.
A comparison is itself an expression whose value is a boolean, so it can appear anywhere a boolean is needed, including on the right of an assignment (boolean ok = x > y;).
Comparisons are the building blocks of conditions: together with boolean logic they provide the basis for decision-making.
Comparisons bind tighter than && and ||, so they are evaluated first and logical operators combine their boolean results.
Comparisons take numbers and produce a boolean; boolean values themselves can be compared only with == and != (not <), and testing them against true is unnecessary.

x = y stores the value of y in x (a statement with a side effect); x == y only tests whether the two values are equal and gives a boolean. Writing = where == is meant is a compile error with int operands and a silent bug with boolean operands.
Used to test a numeric condition: thresholds and sign checks, range tests, divisibility (n % k == 0), loop continuation (i < N), sentinel checks, and running-extreme updates (if (x > max) max = x).

Changing < to <= (or > to >=) changes the result only at the boundary value, which in a loop guard means one more or one fewer iteration (off-by-one); mirroring the comparison (a < b to b > a) preserves the value; negating it gives the complementary operator (!(a < b) is a >= b).

A boolean expression is any expression whose type is boolean: a boolean literal or variable, a comparison, or such parts combined with &&, || and !.

A boolean expression has value true or false; it is built from comparisons (lower precedence than arithmetic, higher than boolean operators) and boolean operators; the condition of if, while and for must be one.

Operands are evaluated left to right; arithmetic sub-expressions first, then comparisons, then !, then &&, then ||; && and || evaluate their right operand only when the left has not decided the result.

Evaluating a boolean expression changes no variable (unless it contains an assignment, ++ or a method with side effects); state changes only when its value is stored, as in isLeapYear = isLeapYear && (year % 100 != 0);.
Comparisons are the atoms of boolean expressions; because they bind tighter than && and ||, month >= 1 && month <= 12 groups as (month >= 1) && (month <= 12) without parentheses.
&&, || and ! combine boolean sub-expressions into a larger one; ! binds tighter than comparisons, so negating a comparison needs parentheses: !(x > 0).
The if statement evaluates its boolean expression once and runs its block only when the value is true; the expression must have type boolean, so if (x = 5) with int x does not compile.

An output statement that names the same variable twice (WRITE y, x, y) prints it only once.
Each expression in the output list is printed, so a repeated variable prints its value each time.
A trace is a table of the values of the program's variables after each statement, used to examine what code does.

A trace has one column per variable and one row per executed statement, in execution order; each row shows the value of every variable after that statement, with a declared but unassigned variable shown as undefined.

Follow the flow of control: take the next statement to execute (re-visiting loop bodies on each pass), evaluate it using the current row's values, and write a new row with the variables it changed; continue until the program ends.
The last row gives the final values (and any printed output follows from them): for int t = a; a = b; b = t; starting from a = 1234, b = 99, the final row is a = 99, b = 1234, t = 1234.
Each row differs from the previous one only in the variable(s) assigned by that statement; all other columns are copied unchanged.
Each assignment statement produces the next row of the trace, changing exactly the column of the variable on its left-hand side.
A test needs an expected result, and the expected result comes from tracing what the program should do, step by step.
Used to check or discover what a piece of code does (e.g. convince yourself that three statements swap a and b) and to debug; tracing a few rows often reveals the purpose of the whole.

A trace shows the effect of a change: reordering the swap's statements (int t = a; b = t; a = b;) produces a different final row in which both variables hold the original a; the trace of the correct swap keeps the invariant that the old value of a is saved in t before a is overwritten.

Trace small or unfamiliar code, loops and suspected bugs by hand; for larger programs, reason about what the parts compute (roles, invariants) or let the program print its variables, since a mental trace can hold only a few values at once.

rule broken: Each row must be computed from the current values, in execution order. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Long traces or loops that overload working memory: stale or wrong values carried into later rows, giving a wrong predicted output.

Identity: an array initializer is a brace-enclosed, comma-separated list of values that creates and fills an array in one step.

Declarative: 'T[] a = {v0, ..., vk};' declares, creates (no new needed) and initializes an array of length k+1. For 2-D arrays each row is its own brace list. The bare form is legal only in a declaration; elsewhere write new T[]{...}.
Sequencing: the array of length k+1 is created, the initializer expressions are evaluated left to right and stored in a[0], a[1], ..., a[k], and then the reference is assigned to a.

items.text: Assignment statement: the statement variable = expression; which stores a data-type value in a variable.

The left-hand side must be a single variable. The right-hand side can be any expression whose type is compatible with the variable's type. = is not mathematical equality (a + b = b + a and 1 = a are illegal).

First the right-hand side is fully evaluated using the variables' current values (left to right). Then that value is stored in the left-hand variable, replacing its old value, and execution moves to the next statement.
As a statement it prints nothing; its result is the new value of the left variable (after c = a + b; with a = 1234 and b = 99, c is 1333). Used as an expression, its value is the value assigned.
Exactly one variable, the left one, changes, and its old value is lost. Variables on the right keep their values: x = x + 5; with x = 5 makes x 10.
The left side must be a declared variable whose type accepts the value. Assignment is how that variable's value changes.
A declaration can include the first assignment (int x = 5;). Assigning to a variable that was never declared does not compile.
Exchanging a[i] and a[j] takes three assignments in a fixed order through a temporary, because each assignment overwrites its target.
int t = a; a = b; b = t; works only in this order, because every assignment destroys its left variable's old value.
x op= e is shorthand for x = x op e. The left variable's current value is fetched first and then combined with e.
Because an assignment is an expression whose value is the value stored, and = groups right to left, a = b = 0 first stores 0 in b and then stores that 0 in a.
As a statement, i++ has the same effect as the assignment i = i + 1.
A trace records the value of each variable after each assignment runs, one row per statement.

x = y stores the value of y in x (a statement with a side effect); x == y only tests whether the two values are equal and gives a boolean. Writing = where == is meant is a compile error with int operands and a silent bug with boolean operands.
Assignment gives a variable its value in each role: initialization, counter update (n = n + 1), gatherer update (sum = sum + x), most-wanted holder update (max = x), or temporary (t = a).

Swapping the two sides (a = b versus b = a) changes which variable changes. Reordering assignments changes the final values. An assignment cannot be undone, because the old value is lost unless it was first saved in a temporary.
